1 Review of Notation and Matrices

1.1 Row Reduction and Echelon Forms

1.1.1 Row Reduction

Definition 1.1.1.1 (Elementary Row Operations)

Elementary row operations are operations that can be performed on the rows of a matrix to transform it into a different form. There are three types of elementary row operations:

  1. Row Switching: Interchanging two rows of the matrix.

  2. Row Multiplication: Multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar.

  3. Row Addition: Adding a multiple of one row to another row.

Definition 1.1.1.2 (Row Echelon Form (REF))

A matrix is said to be in Row Echelon Form (REF) if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. All zero rows (if any) are at the bottom of the matrix.

  2. The leading entry (the first non-zero entry from the left, also called the pivot) of each non-zero row is 1.

  3. The leading entry of a non-zero row is to the right of the leading entry of the previous row.

Elementary row operations can be defined as matrix multiplications. Each elementary row operation can be represented by an elementary matrix, which is obtained by performing the corresponding row operation on an identity matrix. When an elementary matrix is multiplied by another matrix, it performs the same row operation on that matrix.

Definition 1.1.1.3 (Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF))

A matrix is said to be in Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. It is in Row Echelon Form (REF).

  2. The leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is the only non-zero entry in its column.

Theorem 1.1.1.1 (Uniqueness of RREF)

Every matrix is row equivalent to one and only one reduced row echelon matrix.

Proof

Let AA be a matrix. We will show that there exists a unique reduced row echelon form (RREF) matrix RR such that AA is row equivalent to RR.
Existence: We can perform a series of elementary row operations on AA to transform it into its RREF. This process is guaranteed to terminate because each elementary row operation reduces the number of non-zero entries in the matrix, and there are only a finite number of entries in the matrix. Thus, we can always find an RREF matrix RR such that AA is row equivalent to RR.
Uniqueness: Suppose there are two different RREF matrices R1R_1 and R2R_2 such that both are row equivalent to AA. Since both R1R_1 and R2R_2 are in RREF, they must have the same number of leading 1s (pivots) in each column. Furthermore, the positions of these leading 1s must be the same in both matrices because they are determined by the row operations performed on AA. Therefore, R1R_1 and R2R_2 must be identical, which contradicts our assumption that they are different. Hence, there can only be one unique RREF matrix for any given matrix AA.
Thus, we have shown that every matrix is row equivalent to one and only one reduced row echelon matrix. ◻

1.2 Matrix Properties and Subspaces

1.2.1 Matrix Rank, Null Space, and Column Space

Definition 1.2.1.1 (Rank of a Matrix)

The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns in the matrix. It is denoted as rank(A)\text{rank}(A) for a matrix AA. The rank can be determined by transforming the matrix into its Row Echelon Form (REF) or Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) and counting the number of non-zero rows (or leading 1s in RREF).

Definition 1.2.1.2 (Null Space of a Matrix)

The null space (or kernel) of a matrix AA, denoted as null(A)\text{null}(A), is the set of all vectors 𝒙\mathbf{x} such that A𝒙=𝟎A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. In other words, it is the set of all solutions to the homogeneous equation A𝒙=𝟎A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. The null space is a subspace of the vector space ℝn\mathbb{R}^n (or ℂn\mathbb{C}^n) where nn is the number of columns in AA.

Definition 1.2.1.3 (Column Space of a Matrix)

The column space (or range) of a matrix AA, denoted as col(A)\text{col}(A), is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of AA. In other words, it is the set of all vectors that can be expressed as A𝒙A\mathbf{x} for some vector 𝒙\mathbf{x}. The column space is a subspace of the vector space ℝm\mathbb{R}^m (or ℂm\mathbb{C}^m) where mm is the number of rows in AA.

Theorem 1.2.1.1 (Rank-Nullity Theorem)

For any matrix AA of size m×nm \times n, the following relationship holds: rank(A)+null(A)=n\text{rank}(A) + \text{null}(A) = n where rank(A)\text{rank}(A) is the rank of the matrix and null(A)\text{null}(A) is the dimension of the null space of the matrix.

Proof

Let AA be an m×nm \times n matrix. The rank of AA, denoted as rank(A)\text{rank}(A), is the dimension of the column space of AA. The nullity of AA, denoted as null(A)\text{null}(A), is the dimension of the null space of AA. We need to show that rank(A)+null(A)=n\text{rank}(A) + \text{null}(A) = n.

Consider the linear transformation T:ℝn→ℝmT: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m defined by T(𝒙)=A𝒙T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}. The kernel of this transformation is the null space of AA, and the image of this transformation is the column space of AA. By the Rank-Nullity Theorem for linear transformations, we have: dim(ker(T))+dim(im(T))=n\text{dim}(\text{ker}(T)) + \text{dim}(\text{im}(T)) = n where dim(ker(T))=null(A)\text{dim}(\text{ker}(T)) = \text{null}(A) and dim(im(T))=rank(A)\text{dim}(\text{im}(T)) = \text{rank}(A). Therefore, we can rewrite the equation as: null(A)+rank(A)=n\text{null}(A) + \text{rank}(A) = n This completes the proof. ◻

Theorem 1.2.1.2 (Properties of Rank, Null Space, and Column Space)

Let AA and BB be matrices such that the operations are defined. The following properties hold:

  1. Rank of a Product: rank(AB)≤min⁡(rank(A),rank(B))\text{rank}(AB) \leq \min(\text{rank}(A), \text{rank}(B)).

  2. Rank of a Sum: rank(A+B)≤rank(A)+rank(B)\text{rank}(A + B) \leq \text{rank}(A) + \text{rank}(B).

  3. Null Space of a Product: null(AB)⊇null(B)\text{null}(AB) \supseteq \text{null}(B).

  4. Column Space of a Product: col(AB)⊆col(A)\text{col}(AB) \subseteq \text{col}(A).

Proof

We will prove each property one by one.
(1) Rank of a Product: Let AA be an m×nm \times n matrix and BB be an n×pn \times p matrix. The rank of the product ABAB is at most the minimum of the ranks of AA and BB. This is because the column space of ABAB is a subspace of the column space of AA, and the row space of ABAB is a subspace of the row space of BB. Thus, rank(AB)≤min⁡(rank(A),rank(B))\text{rank}(AB) \leq \min(\text{rank}(A), \text{rank}(B)).
(2) Rank of a Sum: Let AA and BB be matrices of the same size. The rank of the sum A+BA + B is at most the sum of the ranks of AA and BB. This follows from the fact that the column space of A+BA + B is contained in the sum of the column spaces of AA and BB. Thus, rank(A+B)≤rank(A)+rank(B)\text{rank}(A + B) \leq \text{rank}(A) + \text{rank}(B).
(3) Null Space of a Product: Let AA be an m×nm \times n matrix and BB be an n×pn \times p matrix. If 𝒙∈null(B)\mathbf{x} \in \text{null}(B), then B𝒙=𝟎B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Therefore, AB𝒙=A𝟎=𝟎AB\mathbf{x} = A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0} which implies that 𝒙∈null(AB)\mathbf{x} \in \text{null}(AB). Thus, null(AB)⊇null(B)\text{null}(AB) \supseteq \text{null}(B).
(4) Column Space of a Product: Let AA be an m×nm \times n matrix and BB be an n×pn \times p matrix. The column space of the product ABAB is contained in the column space of AA. This is because each column of ABAB is a linear combination of the columns of AA. Thus, col(AB)⊆col(A)\text{col}(AB) \subseteq \text{col}(A).
 ◻

Theorem 1.2.1.3 (Column Rank = Row Rank)

For any matrix AA, the dimension of the column space of AA (column rank) is equal to the dimension of the row space of AA (row rank). In other words, rank(A)=rank(AT)\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}(A^T).

Proof

Let AA be an m×nm \times n matrix. The column space of AA, denoted as col(A)\text{col}(A), is the span of the columns of AA. The row space of AA, denoted as row(A)\text{row}(A), is the span of the rows of AA. We need to show that dim(col(A))=dim(row(A))\text{dim}(\text{col}(A)) = \text{dim}(\text{row}(A)).

Consider the linear transformation T:ℝn→ℝmT: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m defined by T(𝒙)=A𝒙T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}. The image of this transformation is the column space of AA, and the kernel of this transformation is the null space of AA. By the Rank-Nullity Theorem, we have: dim(ker(T))+dim(im(T))=n\text{dim}(\text{ker}(T)) + \text{dim}(\text{im}(T)) = n where dim(ker(T))=null(A)\text{dim}(\text{ker}(T)) = \text{null}(A) and dim(im(T))=rank(A)\text{dim}(\text{im}(T)) = \text{rank}(A). Therefore, we can rewrite the equation as: null(A)+rank(A)=n\text{null}(A) + \text{rank}(A) = n

Now, consider the transpose of AA, denoted as ATA^T. The row space of AA is equivalent to the column space of ATA^T. By applying the same reasoning to ATA^T, we have: null(AT)+rank(AT)=m\text{null}(A^T) + \text{rank}(A^T) = m

Since the rank of a matrix is equal to the rank of its transpose, we have rank(A)=rank(AT)\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}(A^T). Thus, we can conclude that: dim(col(A))=rank(A)=rank(AT)=dim(row(A))\text{dim}(\text{col}(A)) = \text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}(A^T) = \text{dim}(\text{row}(A))

Therefore, we have shown that the dimension of the column space of AA is equal to the dimension of the row space of AA, i.e., rank(A)=rank(AT)\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}(A^T). ◻

Note 1.2.1.1

The rank of a matrix provides important information about the linear independence of its rows and columns, as well as the solutions to systems of linear equations associated with the matrix. The null space and column space are fundamental concepts in linear algebra that help us understand the structure of linear transformations and their effects on vector spaces.

1.3 Mappings from ℝn\mathbb{R}^n to ℝ\mathbb{R} and Invertibility

1.3.1 Determinants, Inverses, Transposes, and Traces

Definition 1.3.1.1 (Determinant of a Matrix)

The determinant of a matrix A∈MnFA \in M_n{F} is a function det⁡:MnF→F\det: M_n{F} \to F that satisfies the following properties:

  1. Multilinearity: The determinant is a linear function in each row of the matrix. This means that if we fix all rows except one, the determinant behaves like a linear function with respect to that row.

  2. Alternating Property: If two rows of the matrix are identical, then the determinant is zero. This property ensures that the determinant changes sign when two rows are swapped.

  3. Normalization: The determinant of the identity matrix InI_n is 1, i.e., det⁡(In)=1\det(I_n) = 1.

  4. Row Operations: The determinant changes in specific ways under elementary row operations:

    • Swapping two rows multiplies the determinant by -1.

    • Multiplying a row by a scalar kk multiplies the determinant by kk.

    • Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant.

Note 1.3.1.1

The determinant can be computed using various methods, including cofactor expansion, row reduction, and properties of determinants. The determinant is a useful tool in linear algebra for determining the invertibility of a matrix, calculating areas and volumes, and solving systems of linear equations.

We define the determinant recursively using minors and cofactors. For a 2×22 \times 2 matrix, the determinant is given by: det⁡(abcd)=ad−bc\det\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix} = ad - bc For a general n×nn \times n matrix A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}), the determinant is defined as: det⁡(A)=∑j=1na1jC1j\boxed{ \det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{1j} C_{1j}} where C1jC_{1j} is the cofactor of the element a1ja_{1j}, defined as: C1j=(−1)1+jdet⁡(M1j)C_{1j} = (-1)^{1+j} \det(M_{1j}) and M1jM_{1j} is the (n−1)×(n−1)(n-1) \times (n-1) minor matrix obtained by deleting the first row and the jj-th column of AA.

Theorem 1.3.1.1 (Properties of Determinants)

Let AA and BB be square matrices of size n×nn \times n. The following properties hold:

  1. Multiplicative Property: det⁡(AB)=det⁡(A)det⁡(B)\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B).

  2. Transpose Property: det⁡(AT)=det⁡(A)\det(A^T) = \det(A).

  3. Effect of Row Operations: - Swapping two rows of AA multiplies the determinant by −1-1. - Multiplying a row of AA by a scalar cc multiplies the determinant by cc. - Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant.

  4. Determinant of Identity Matrix: det⁡(In)=1\det(I_n) = 1, where InI_n is the identity matrix of size n×nn \times n.

  5. Determinant of Triangular Matrix: If AA is a triangular matrix (upper or lower), then det⁡(A)\det(A) is the product of its diagonal entries.

  6. Invertibility: A matrix AA is invertible if and only if det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0.

Proof

We will prove each property one by one.
(1) Multiplicative Property: Let AA and BB be square matrices of size n×nn \times n. The determinant of the product of two matrices can be computed using the definition of the determinant as a sum over permutations. By expanding both det⁡(AB)\det(AB) and det⁡(A)det⁡(B)\det(A)\det(B) using this definition, we can show that they are equal. This is a standard result in linear algebra and can be found in most textbooks.
(2) Transpose Property: The determinant of a matrix is equal to the determinant of its transpose. This can be shown by noting that the definition of the determinant involves summing over permutations of the indices, and transposing the matrix does not change the set of permutations or their signs. Thus, det⁡(AT)=det⁡(A)\det(A^T) = \det(A).
(3) Effect of Row Operations: - Swapping two rows of a matrix changes the sign of the determinant. This can be shown by considering the effect of the row swap on the permutations in the determinant definition. - Multiplying a row by a scalar cc multiplies the determinant by cc. This follows from the linearity of the determinant with respect to each row. - Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant. This is because such an operation can be viewed as a linear combination of rows, which does not affect the overall sum in the determinant definition.
(4) Determinant of Identity Matrix: The identity matrix InI_n has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. The only permutation that contributes to the determinant is the identity permutation, which has a sign of 1. Thus, det⁡(In)=1\det(I_n) = 1.
(5) Determinant of Triangular Matrix: For a triangular matrix (upper or lower), the determinant can be computed as the product of its diagonal entries. This is because the only permutations that contribute to the determinant are those that select all diagonal entries, and each such permutation has a sign of 1. Thus, det⁡(A)\det(A) is the product of the diagonal entries.
(6) Invertibility: A matrix AA is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero. If det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0, then there exists a matrix A−1A^{-1} such that AA−1=InAA^{-1} = I_n. Conversely, if AA is invertible, then det⁡(A)det⁡(A−1)=det⁡(In)=1\det(A)\det(A^{-1}) = \det(I_n) = 1, which implies that det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0. ◻

Definition 1.3.1.2 (Invertible Matrix)

A square matrix AA is said to be invertible (or non-singular) if there exists a matrix A−1A^{-1} such that AA−1=A−1A=InAA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I_n, where InI_n is the identity matrix of size n×nn \times n.

Theorem 1.3.1.2 (Invertibility Theorem)

For a square matrix AA of size n×nn \times n, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. AA is invertible (i.e., there exists a matrix A−1A^{-1} such that AA−1=A−1A=InAA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I_n, where InI_n is the identity matrix of size n×nn \times n).

  2. The determinant of AA is non-zero (i.e., det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0).

  3. The rank of AA is nn (i.e., rank(A)=n\text{rank}(A) = n).

  4. The null space of AA contains only the zero vector (i.e., null(A)={𝟎}\text{null}(A) = \{ \mathbf{0} \}).

  5. The column space of AA is ℝn\mathbb{R}^n (or ℂn\mathbb{C}^n) (i.e., col(A)=ℝn\text{col}(A) = \mathbb{R}^n or ℂn\mathbb{C}^n).

  6. The rows of AA are linearly independent.

  7. The columns of AA are linearly independent.

Proof

We will show that each statement implies the next, and finally that the last statement implies the first, thus proving their equivalence.
(1) ⇒\Rightarrow (2): If AA is invertible, then there exists a matrix A−1A^{-1} such that AA−1=InAA^{-1} = I_n. Taking the determinant of both sides, we have: det⁡(AA−1)=det⁡(In)⟹det⁡(A)det⁡(A−1)=1⟹det⁡(A)≠0\det(AA^{-1}) = \det(I_n) \implies \det(A)\det(A^{-1}) = 1 \implies \det(A) \neq 0 (2) ⇒\Rightarrow (3): If det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0, then AA has full rank, which means rank(A)=n\text{rank}(A) = n.
(3) ⇒\Rightarrow (4): If rank(A)=n\text{rank}(A) = n, then the null space of AA contains only the zero vector. This is because if there were a non-zero vector in the null space, it would imply that the columns of AA are linearly dependent by the rank-nullity theorem, contradicting the fact that rank(A)=n\text{rank}(A) = n.
(4) ⇒\Rightarrow (5): If the null space of AA contains only the zero vector, then the column space of AA must be all of ℝn\mathbb{R}^n (or ℂn\mathbb{C}^n). This is because if there were a vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^n (or ℂn\mathbb{C}^n) that could not be expressed as a linear combination of the columns of AA, it would imply that there is a non-zero vector in the null space.
(5) ⇒\Rightarrow (6): If the column space of AA is ℝn\mathbb{R}^n (or ℂn\mathbb{C}^n), then the rows of AA must be linearly independent. This is because if the rows were linearly dependent, it would imply that there is a non-zero vector in the null space.
(6) ⇒\Rightarrow (7): If the rows of AA are linearly independent, then the columns of AA must also be linearly independent. This is because the rank of AA is equal to the number of linearly independent rows, which is nn.
(7) ⇒\Rightarrow (1): If the columns of AA are linearly independent, then AA has full rank, which means rank(A)=n\text{rank}(A) = n. This implies that AA is invertible. Thus, we have shown that each statement implies the next, and finally that the last statement implies the first, proving their equivalence. ◻

Definition 1.3.1.3 (Transpose of a Matrix)

The transpose of a matrix AA, denoted as ATA^T, is obtained by swapping the rows and columns of AA. If AA is an m×nm \times n matrix, then its transpose ATA^T is an n×mn \times m matrix defined by: (AT)ij=Aji(A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}

Theorem 1.3.1.3 (Properties of Transpose)

Let AA and BB be matrices such that the operations are defined. The following properties hold:

  1. Double Transpose: (AT)T=A(A^T)^T = A.

  2. Transpose of a Sum: (A+B)T=AT+BT(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T.

  3. Transpose of a Scalar Multiple: (cA)T=cAT(cA)^T = cA^T for any scalar cc.

  4. Transpose of a Product: (AB)T=BTAT(AB)^T = B^T A^T.

  5. Transpose of an Inverse: If AA is invertible, then (A−1)T=(AT)−1(A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1}.

Proof

We provide matrix proofs for each property.
(1) Double Transpose: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}). Then, (AT)ijT=(AT)ji=aij(A^T)^T_{ij} = (A^T)_{ji} = a_{ij} Thus, (AT)T=A(A^T)^T = A.
(2) Transpose of a Sum: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}) and B=(bij)B = (b_{ij}). Then, (A+B)ijT=(A+B)ji=aji+bji=AijT+BijT(A + B)^T_{ij} = (A + B)_{ji} = a_{ji} + b_{ji} = A^T_{ij} + B^T_{ij} Thus, (A+B)T=AT+BT(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T.
(3) Transpose of a Scalar Multiple: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}) and cc be a scalar. Then, (cA)ijT=(cA)ji=caji=cAijT(cA)^T_{ij} = (cA)_{ji} = c a_{ji} = c A^T_{ij} Thus, (cA)T=cAT(cA)^T = cA^T.
(4) Transpose of a Product: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}) and B=(bij)B = (b_{ij}). Then, (AB)ijT=(AB)ji=∑kajkbki=∑kbkiajk=(BTAT)ij(AB)^T_{ij} = (AB)_{ji} = \sum_{k} a_{jk} b_{ki} = \sum_{k} b_{ki} a_{jk} = (B^T A^T)_{ij} Thus, (AB)T=BTAT(AB)^T = B^T A^T.
(5) Transpose of an Inverse: If AA is invertible, then AA−1=InAA^{-1} = I_n. Taking the transpose of both sides, we have: (AA−1)T=(In)T⟹(A−1)TAT=In⟹(A−1)T=(AT)−1(AA^{-1})^T = (I_n)^T \implies (A^{-1})^T A^T = I_n \implies (A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1} Thus, (A−1)T=(AT)−1(A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1}. ◻

Definition 1.3.1.4 (Trace of a Matrix)

The trace of a square matrix AA of size n×nn \times n, denoted as tr(A)\text{tr}(A), is defined as the sum of its diagonal elements. Mathematically, it is given by: tr(A)=∑i=1naii\text{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} where aiia_{ii} are the diagonal elements of the matrix AA.

Theorem 1.3.1.4 (Properties of Trace)

Let AA and BB be square matrices of size n×nn \times n. The following properties hold:

  1. Linearity: tr(A+B)=tr(A)+tr(B)\text{tr}(A + B) = \text{tr}(A) + \text{tr}(B) and tr(cA)=ctr(A)\text{tr}(cA) = c\text{tr}(A) for any scalar cc.

  2. Cyclic Property: tr(AB)=tr(BA)\text{tr}(AB) = \text{tr}(BA).

  3. Invariance under Similarity Transformations: If B=P−1APB = P^{-1}AP for some invertible matrix PP, then tr(B)=tr(A)\text{tr}(B) = \text{tr}(A).

  4. Trace of Identity Matrix: tr(In)=n\text{tr}(I_n) = n, where InI_n is the identity matrix of size n×nn \times n.

  5. Trace of a Transpose: tr(AT)=tr(A)\text{tr}(A^T) = \text{tr}(A).

Proof

We provide matrix proofs for each property.
(1) Linearity: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}) and B=(bij)B = (b_{ij}). Then, tr(A+B)=∑i=1n(aii+bii)=∑i=1naii+∑i=1nbii=tr(A)+tr(B)\text{tr}(A + B) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_{ii} + b_{ii}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{ii} = \text{tr}(A) + \text{tr}(B) and for a scalar cc, tr(cA)=∑i=1n(caii)=c∑i=1naii=ctr(A).\text{tr}(cA) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (ca_{ii}) = c\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} = c\text{tr}(A).
(2) Cyclic Property: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}) and B=(bij)B = (b_{ij}). Then, tr(AB)=∑i=1n(AB)ii=∑i=1n∑j=1naijbji=∑j=1n∑i=1nbjiaij=tr(BA).\text{tr}(AB) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (AB)_{ii} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}b_{ji} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_{ji}a_{ij} = \text{tr}(BA). (3) Invariance under Similarity Transformations: Let B=P−1APB = P^{-1}AP. Then, tr(B)=tr(P−1AP)=tr(APP−1)=tr(A)\text{tr}(B) = \text{tr}(P^{-1}AP) = \text{tr}(AP P^{-1}) = \text{tr}(A) using the cyclic property of the trace.
(4) Trace of Identity Matrix: The identity matrix InI_n has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Thus, tr(In)=∑i=1n1=n.\text{tr}(I_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n. (5) Trace of a Transpose: Let A=(aij)A = (a_{ij}). Then, tr(AT)=∑i=1n(AT)ii=∑i=1naji=∑j=1najj=tr(A).\text{tr}(A^T) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (A^T)_{ii} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ji} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{jj} = \text{tr}(A). ◻

Theorem 1.3.1.5 (Sum of Eigenvalues is equal to Trace)

Let AA be a square matrix of size n×nn \times n. Then, the sum of the eigenvalues of AA is equal to the trace of AA: ∑i=1nλi=tr(A)\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i = \text{tr}(A) where λ1,λ2,…,λn\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n are the eigenvalues of AA.

Proof

Let AA be a square matrix of size n×nn \times n with eigenvalues λ1,λ2,…,λn\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n. The characteristic polynomial of AA is given by: p(λ)=det⁡(A−λI)=(−1)n(λn−cn−1λn−1+cn−2λn−2−…+(−1)nc0)p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) = (-1)^n (\lambda^n - c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + c_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2} - \ldots + (-1)^n c_0) where cn−1,cn−2,…,c0c_{n-1}, c_{n-2}, \ldots, c_0 are coefficients that depend on the entries of AA. The eigenvalues of AA are the roots of the characteristic polynomial. By Vieta’s formulas, the sum of the roots (eigenvalues) of the polynomial is equal to the coefficient of λn−1\lambda^{n-1} divided by the coefficient of λn\lambda^n, with a sign change. Thus, ∑i=1nλi=cn−1\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i = c_{n-1} Now, we need to show that cn−1=tr(A)c_{n-1} = \text{tr}(A). The coefficient cn−1c_{n-1} can be computed as the sum of the principal minors of order 1 of the matrix AA, which is simply the sum of the diagonal elements of AA. Therefore, cn−1=∑i=1naii=tr(A)c_{n-1} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} = \text{tr}(A) Combining these results, we have: ∑i=1nλi=cn−1=tr(A)\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i = c_{n-1} = \text{tr}(A) Thus, we have shown that the sum of the eigenvalues of AA is equal to the trace of AA. ◻

1.3.2 Symmetric, Skew Symmetric, Triangular Matrices

Definition 1.3.2.1 (Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices)

A square matrix AA is called symmetric if it is equal to its transpose, i.e., A=ATA = A^T. A square matrix AA is called skew-symmetric if it is equal to the negative of its transpose, i.e., A=−ATA = -A^T.

Theorem 1.3.2.1 (Decomposition of a Matrix into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Parts)

Any square matrix AA can be uniquely expressed as the sum of a symmetric matrix SS and a skew-symmetric matrix KK. Specifically, we can write: A=S+KA = S + K where S=12(A+AT)andK=12(A−AT)S = \frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) \quad \text{and} \quad K = \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T)

Proof

Let AA be a square matrix. We define the symmetric part SS and the skew-symmetric part KK as follows: S=12(A+AT)andK=12(A−AT)S = \frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) \quad \text{and} \quad K = \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T) First, we will show that SS is symmetric: ST=(12(A+AT))T=12(AT+(AT)T)=12(AT+A)=SS^T = \left(\frac{1}{2}(A + A^T)\right)^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T + (A^T)^T) = \frac{1}{2}(A^T + A) = S Thus, SS is symmetric. Next, we will show that KK is skew-symmetric: KT=(12(A−AT))T=12(AT−(AT)T)=12(AT−A)=−KK^T = \left(\frac{1}{2}(A - A^T)\right)^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T - (A^T)^T) = \frac{1}{2}(A^T - A) = -K Thus, KK is skew-symmetric. Now, we will show that AA can be expressed as the sum of SS and KK: S+K=12(A+AT)+12(A−AT)=12(2A)=AS + K = \frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T) = \frac{1}{2}(2A) = A Finally, we need to show that this decomposition is unique. Suppose there exist another symmetric matrix S′S' and another skew-symmetric matrix K′K' such that: A=S′+K′A = S' + K' Then, S+K=S′+K′⟹S−S′=K′−KS + K = S' + K' \implies S - S' = K' - K The left side of the equation is symmetric, and the right side is skew-symmetric. The only matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric is the zero matrix. Therefore, S−S′=0andK′−K=0S - S' = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad K' - K = 0 which implies that S=S′S = S' and K=K′K = K'. Thus, the decomposition is unique. ◻

Theorem 1.3.2.2 (Properties of Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices)

Let AA and BB be square matrices of size n×nn \times n. The following properties hold:

  1. The sum of two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

  2. The sum of two skew-symmetric matrices is skew-symmetric.

  3. The product of two symmetric matrices is symmetric if and only if they commute, i.e., AB=BAAB = BA.

  4. The product of two skew-symmetric matrices is symmetric if and only if they commute, i.e., AB=BAAB = BA.

  5. The product of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix is skew-symmetric.

  6. The trace of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero.

Proof

We provide matrix proofs for each property.
(1) Sum of Symmetric Matrices: Let AA and BB be symmetric matrices. Then, (A+B)T=AT+BT=A+B(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T = A + B Thus, A+BA + B is symmetric.
(2) Sum of Skew-Symmetric Matrices: Let AA and BB be skew-symmetric matrices. Then, (A+B)T=AT+BT=−A−B=−(A+B)(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T = -A - B = -(A + B) Thus, A+BA + B is skew-symmetric.
(3) Product of Symmetric Matrices: Let AA and BB be symmetric matrices. Then, (AB)T=BTAT=BA(AB)^T = B^T A^T = BA Thus, ABAB is symmetric if and only if AB=BAAB = BA.
(4) Product of Skew-Symmetric Matrices: Let AA and BB be skew-symmetric matrices. Then, (AB)T=BTAT=(−B)(−A)=BA(AB)^T = B^T A^T = (-B)(-A) = BA Thus, ABAB is symmetric if and only if AB=BAAB = BA.
(5) Product of Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices: Let AA be a symmetric matrix and BB be a skew-symmetric matrix. Then, (AB)T=BTAT=(−B)A=−BA(AB)^T = B^T A^T = (-B)A = -BA Thus, ABAB is skew-symmetric.
(6) Trace of Skew-Symmetric Matrix: Let AA be a skew-symmetric matrix. Then, tr(A)=∑i=1naii\text{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} Since AA is skew-symmetric, we have aii=−aiia_{ii} = -a_{ii} for all diagonal elements, which implies that aii=0a_{ii} = 0. Therefore, tr(A)=∑i=1n0=0\text{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 0 = 0 ◻

Definition 1.3.2.2 (Triangular Matrices)

A square matrix AA is called upper triangular if all the entries below the main diagonal are zero, i.e., aij=0a_{ij} = 0 for all i>ji > j. A square matrix AA is called lower triangular if all the entries above the main diagonal are zero, i.e., aij=0a_{ij} = 0 for all i<ji < j.

Theorem 1.3.2.3 (Properties of Triangular Matrices)

Let AA and BB be square matrices of size n×nn \times n. The following properties hold:

  1. The sum of two upper triangular matrices is upper triangular.

  2. The sum of two lower triangular matrices is lower triangular.

  3. The product of two upper triangular matrices is upper triangular.

  4. The product of two lower triangular matrices is lower triangular.

  5. The inverse of an invertible upper triangular matrix is upper triangular.

  6. The inverse of an invertible lower triangular matrix is lower triangular.

  7. The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

  8. The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are the entries on its main diagonal.

Proof

We provide matrix proofs for each property.
(1) Sum of Upper Triangular Matrices: Let AA and BB be upper triangular matrices. Then, for all i>ji > j, (A+B)ij=aij+bij=0+0=0(A + B)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij} = 0 + 0 = 0 Thus, A+BA + B is upper triangular.
(2) Sum of Lower Triangular Matrices: Let AA and BB be lower triangular matrices. Then, for all i<ji < j, (A+B)ij=aij+bij=0+0=0(A + B)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij} = 0 + 0 = 0 Thus, A+BA + B is lower triangular.
(3) Product of Upper Triangular Matrices: Let AA and BB be upper triangular matrices. Then, for all i>ji > j, (AB)ij=∑k=1naikbkj(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik}b_{kj} Since aik=0a_{ik} = 0 for all k<ik < i and bkj=0b_{kj} = 0 for all k>jk > j, the only non-zero terms in the sum occur when k≥ik \geq i and k≤jk \leq j. If i>ji > j, there are no such kk, so (AB)ij=0(AB)_{ij} = 0. Thus, ABAB is upper triangular.
(4) Product of Lower Triangular Matrices: Let AA and BB be lower triangular matrices. Then, for all i<ji < j, (AB)ij=∑k=1naikbkj(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik}b_{kj} Since aik=0a_{ik} = 0 for all k>ik > i and bkj=0b_{kj} = 0 for all k<jk < j, the only non-zero terms in the sum occur when k≤ik \leq i and k≥jk \geq j. If i<ji < j, there are no such kk, so (AB)ij=0(AB)_{ij} = 0. Thus, ABAB is lower triangular.
(5) Inverse of Upper Triangular Matrix: Let AA be an invertible upper triangular matrix. We can find its inverse A−1A^{-1} using the method of back substitution. The resulting matrix A−1A^{-1} will also be upper triangular because the process of finding the inverse does not introduce any non-zero entries below the main diagonal.
(6) Inverse of Lower Triangular Matrix: Let AA be an invertible lower triangular matrix. We can find its inverse A−1A^{-1} using the method of forward substitution. The resulting matrix A−1A^{-1} will also be lower triangular because the process of finding the inverse does not introduce any non-zero entries above the main diagonal.
(7) Determinant of Triangular Matrix: Let AA be a triangular matrix. The determinant of AA can be computed as the product of its diagonal entries. This is because the only permutations that contribute to the determinant are those that select all diagonal entries, and each such permutation has a sign of 1. Thus, det⁡(A)=∏i=1naii\det(A) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} (8) Eigenvalues of Triangular Matrix: Let AA be a triangular matrix. The eigenvalues of AA are the entries on its main diagonal. This can be shown by considering the characteristic polynomial of AA, which is given by: det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(A - \lambda I) = 0 Since AA is triangular, A−λIA - \lambda I is also triangular, and its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries: det⁡(A−λI)=∏i=1n(aii−λ)\det(A - \lambda I) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (a_{ii} - \lambda) Setting this equal to zero, we find that the eigenvalues are the solutions to the equation aii−λ=0a_{ii} - \lambda = 0 for each ii, which gives λ=aii\lambda = a_{ii}. Thus, the eigenvalues of AA are the entries on its main diagonal. ◻

2 Groups and Vector Spaces

2.1 Groups

2.1.1 Laws of Composition

Definition 2.1.1.1 (Laws of Composition)

A law of composition on a set SS is a function which combines any two elements of the set and gives another element of the set. Formally, a law of composition on SS is a function - *:S×S→S*: S \times S \to S which takes two elements a,b∈Sa, b \in S and gives another element c∈Sc \in S such that c=a*bc = a * b. A law of composition is a binary operation on the set SS and is often denoted by symbols like **, ++, or ⋅\cdot.

Example 2.1.1.1

In context of linear algebra, consider the set of all n×nn \times n matrices over a field FF. The law of composition is matrix multiplication, which takes two matrices A,B∈Fn×nA, B \in F^{n \times n} and gives another matrix C∈Fn×nC \in F^{n \times n} such that C=A*BC = A * B. We will later see that such a set with certain restrictions forms a group.

Definition 2.1.1.2 (Monoids)

A monoid is a set MM with a law of composition ** such that:

  1. Closure: For all a,b∈Ma, b \in M, a*b∈Ma * b \in M.

  2. Associativity: For all a,b,c∈Ma, b, c \in M, (a*b)*c=a*(b*c)(a * b) * c = a * (b * c).

  3. Identity Element: There exists an element e∈Me \in M such that for all a∈Ma \in M, e*a=a*e=ae * a = a * e = a.

Example 2.1.1.2

The set of natural numbers ℕ∪{0}\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} under addition forms a monoid. The identity element is 00, and the operation is associative. However, it does not have inverses for all elements, so it is not a group.

Definition 2.1.1.3 (Groups)

A group is a set GG with a law of composition ** such that the following properties hold:

  1. Closure: For all a,b∈Ga, b \in G, a*b∈Ga * b \in G.

  2. Associativity: For all a,b,c∈Ga, b, c \in G, (a*b)*c=a*(b*c)(a * b) * c = a * (b * c).

  3. Identity Element: There exists an element e∈Ge \in G such that for all a∈Ga \in G, e*a=a*e=ae * a = a * e = a.

  4. Inverse Element: For every element a∈Ga \in G, there exists an element b∈Gb \in G such that a*b=b*a=ea * b = b * a = e.

Example 2.1.1.3

The set of all n×nn \times n invertible matrices over a field FF, denoted as GL(n,F)GL(n, F), forms a group under matrix multiplication. The identity element is the identity matrix InI_n, and the inverse of a matrix AA is its inverse A−1A^{-1} such that A*A−1=InA * A^{-1} = I_n.

Note 2.1.1.1

Note: The set of all n×nn \times n matrices does not form a group under matrix multiplication because not all matrices are invertible. However, the set of invertible matrices does satisfy all the group properties.

Definition 2.1.1.4

Abelian Groups A group GG is called an Abelian group if the law of composition is commutative, i.e., for all a,b∈Ga, b \in G, a*b=b*aa * b = b * a.

Example 2.1.1.4

The set of all n×nn \times n invertible matrices over a field FF does not form an Abelian group under matrix multiplication because matrix multiplication is not commutative in general. However, the set of all n×nn \times n diagonal matrices with non-zero entries forms an Abelian group under matrix multiplication.

Example 2.1.1.5

The set of all integers ℤ\mathbb{Z} under addition forms an Abelian group. The identity element is 00, and the inverse of any integer aa is −a-a such that a+(−a)=0a + (-a) = 0.

Example 2.1.1.6

A vector space over a field FF can be viewed as an Abelian group under vector addition. The identity element is the zero vector, and the inverse of any vector 𝒗\mathbf{v} is −𝒗-\mathbf{v} such that 𝒗+(−𝒗)=𝟎\mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}.

Definition 2.1.1.5 (Rings)

A ring is a set RR with two binary operations, addition ++ and multiplication ⋅\cdot, such that:

  1. Additive Group: (R,+)(R, +) is an Abelian group, meaning it satisfies closure, associativity, commutativity, has an identity element (zero), and every element has an additive inverse.

  2. Multiplication: The multiplication operation ⋅\cdot is associative and distributes over addition, i.e., for all a,b,c∈Ra, b, c \in R, a⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅ca \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c and (a+b)⋅c=a⋅c+b⋅c(a + b) \cdot c = a \cdot c + b \cdot c.

  3. Multiplicative Closure: For all a,b∈Ra, b \in R, a⋅b∈Ra \cdot b \in R.

  4. Multiplicative Identity (optional): If there exists an element 1∈R1 \in R such that for all a∈Ra \in R, 1⋅a=a⋅1=a1 \cdot a = a \cdot 1 = a, then RR is called a unital ring.

Example 2.1.1.7

The set of integers ℤ\mathbb{Z} forms a ring under the usual addition and multiplication. It has an additive identity (zero) and a multiplicative identity (one). The integers are closed under both operations, and multiplication distributes over addition.

Example 2.1.1.8

The set of all n×nn \times n matrices over a field FF forms a ring under matrix addition and multiplication. It has an additive identity (the zero matrix) and a multiplicative identity (the identity matrix). However, it is not commutative under multiplication in general.

Example 2.1.1.9

The set of integers modulo nn, denoted ℤ/nℤ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, forms a ring under addition and multiplication modulo nn. It has an additive identity (the equivalence class of zero) and a multiplicative identity (the equivalence class of one). The operations are well-defined and satisfy the ring properties.

Definition 2.1.1.6 (Fields)

A field is a set FF with two binary operations, addition ++ and multiplication ⋅\cdot, such that:

  1. Additive Group: (F,+)(F, +) is an Abelian group, meaning it satisfies closure, associativity, commutativity, has an identity element (zero), and every element has an additive inverse.

  2. Multiplicative Group: (F\{0},⋅)(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot) is an Abelian group, meaning it satisfies closure, associativity, commutativity, has an identity element (one), and every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse.

  3. Distributive Property: Multiplication distributes over addition, i.e., for all a,b,c∈Fa, b, c \in F, a⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅ca \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c and (a+b)⋅c=a⋅c+b⋅c(a + b) \cdot c = a \cdot c + b \cdot c.

Example 2.1.1.10

The set of rational numbers ℚ\mathbb{Q} forms a field under the usual addition and multiplication. It has an additive identity (zero) and a multiplicative identity (one). Every non-zero rational number has a multiplicative inverse, and the operations are commutative and associative.

Example 2.1.1.11

The set of real numbers ℝ\mathbb{R} forms a field under the usual addition and multiplication. It has an additive identity (zero) and a multiplicative identity (one). Every non-zero real number has a multiplicative inverse, and the operations are commutative and associative.

Definition 2.1.1.7 (Subgroups)

A subset HH of a group GG is called a subgroup if it is itself a group under the same law of composition as GG. This means that:

  1. HH is non-empty.

  2. For all a,b∈Ha, b \in H, a*b∈Ha * b \in H (closure).

  3. For all a∈Ha \in H, there exists an inverse b∈Hb \in H such that a*b=ea * b = e (identity and inverse).

2.1.2 Finite Groups

Definition 2.1.2.1 (Finite Groups)

A group GG is called a finite group if it has a finite number of elements. Finite groups have specific interesting properties, such as:

  1. Every subgroup of a finite group is also finite.

  2. Elements of a finite group have finite order, meaning for each element a∈Ga \in G, there exists a positive integer nn such that an=ea^n = e, where ee is the identity element.

  3. Finite groups can be classified into simple groups, solvable groups, and more.

Example 2.1.2.1

The group of integers modulo nn, denoted ℤ/nℤ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, is a finite group under addition modulo nn. The order of this group is nn, and it has subgroups corresponding to the divisors of nn.

Example 2.1.2.2

The group of invertible matrices GL(n,ℤ/pℤ)GL(n, \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}) is a finite group under matrix multiplication.

Theorem 2.1.2.1 (Cancellation Law)

In a group GG, if a,b,c∈Ga, b, c \in G and a*b=a*ca * b = a * c, then b=cb = c. Similarly, if b*a=c*ab * a = c * a, then b=cb = c.

Proof

The cancellation law follows from the existence of inverses in a group and the associativity of the group operation. If a*b=a*ca * b = a * c, we can multiply both sides by a−1a^{-1} (the inverse of aa) to get b=cb = c. Similarly, if b*a=c*ab * a = c * a, multiplying both sides by a−1a^{-1} gives b=cb = c. ◻

2.2 Vector Spaces

We study vector spaces, which are fundamental structures in linear algebra. A vector space is a set of vectors that can be added together and multiplied by scalars, satisfying certain axioms. We shall look at subspaces of ℝn\mathbb{R}^n and ℂn\mathbb{C}^n, which are the most common examples of vector spaces.

2.2.1 Vector Spaces

Definition 2.2.1.1 (Vector Space)

A vector space over a field FF is a set VV equipped with two operations: vector addition and scalar multiplication, satisfying the following axioms:

  1. Closure under Addition: For all 𝒖,𝒗∈V\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V, 𝒖+𝒗∈V\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \in V.

  2. Associativity of Addition: For all 𝒖,𝒗,𝒘∈V\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V, (𝒖+𝒗)+𝒘=𝒖+(𝒗+𝒘)(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}).

  3. Commutativity of Addition: For all 𝒖,𝒗∈V\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V, 𝒖+𝒗=𝒗+𝒖\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}.

  4. Existence of Zero Vector: There exists a vector 𝟎∈V\mathbf{0} \in V such that for all 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V, 𝒗+𝟎=𝒗\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v}.

  5. Existence of Additive Inverses: For every vector 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V, there exists a vector −𝒗∈V-\mathbf{v} \in V such that 𝒗+(−𝒗)=𝟎\mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}.

  6. Closure under Scalar Multiplication: For all c∈Fc \in F and 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V, c𝒗∈Vc\mathbf{v} \in V.

  7. Distributive Property: - For all c,d∈Fc, d \in F and 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V, (c+d)𝒗=c𝒗+d𝒗(c + d)\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{v} + d\mathbf{v}. - For all c∈Fc \in F and 𝒖,𝒗∈V\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V, c(𝒖+𝒗)=c𝒖+c𝒗c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v}.

  8. Associativity of Scalar Multiplication: - For all c,d∈Fc, d \in F and 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V, (cd)𝒗=c(d𝒗)(cd)\mathbf{v} = c(d\mathbf{v}).

Note 2.2.1.1

The zero vector 𝟎\mathbf{0} is unique in a vector space, and it serves as the identity element for vector addition. The additive inverse −𝒗-\mathbf{v} is also unique for each vector 𝒗\mathbf{v}.
Any vector space forms an Abelian group under vector addition, and scalar multiplication is compatible with the field operations.

Example 2.2.1.1

The set of all nn-tuples of real numbers ℝn\mathbb{R}^n forms a vector space over the field of real numbers ℝ\mathbb{R}. The zero vector is the nn-tuple of zeros, and scalar multiplication is defined as multiplying each component by a scalar.

Example 2.2.1.2

The set of all polynomials with real coefficients forms a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R}. The zero vector is the zero polynomial, and scalar multiplication is defined as multiplying the polynomial by a real number.

Example 2.2.1.3

The set of all continuous functions defined on a closed interval [a,b][a, b] forms a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R}. The zero vector is the zero function, and scalar multiplication is defined as multiplying the function by a real number.

Example 2.2.1.4

The set of all n×mn \times m matrices with real entries forms a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R}. The zero vector is the zero matrix, and scalar multiplication is defined as multiplying each entry of the matrix by a real number.

Definition 2.2.1.2 (Subspace)

A subset WW of a vector space VV is called a subspace if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. WW is non-empty (contains the zero vector).

  2. WW is closed under vector addition: For all 𝒖,𝒗∈W\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W, 𝒖+𝒗∈W\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \in W.

  3. WW is closed under scalar multiplication: For all c∈Fc \in F and 𝒗∈W\mathbf{v} \in W, c𝒗∈Wc\mathbf{v} \in W.

Note 2.2.1.2

A subspace of a vector space is itself a vector space under the same operations. The zero vector of the parent vector space is also the zero vector of the subspace.
Subspaces can be thought of as "smaller" vector spaces contained within a larger vector space, although this makes sense only when the larger vector space is non-trivial (i.e., it contains more than just the zero vector), and the subspace is not the entire vector space.

Theorem 2.2.1.1 (Conditions for Subspace)

A non-empty subset of a vector space VV is a subspace if and only if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. In other words, if and only if W⊆VW \subseteq V is non-empty and for each pair of vectors 𝒖,𝒗∈W\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W and for each scalar c∈𝔽c \in \mathbb{F}, we have c𝒖+𝒘∈Wc\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} \in W, then WW is a subspace of VV.

Proof

Let W⊆VW \subseteq V be a non-empty subset. We need to show that WW is a subspace if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. We show that if these three properties are satisfied, then all other properties of a vector space are also satisfied.

  1. Non-Empty - Since WW is non-empty, it contains at least one vector 𝒗\mathbf{v}. Thus, WW is non-empty.

  2. Closure under addition - Let 𝒖,𝒗∈W\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W. Since WW is closed under vector addition, we have 𝒖+𝒗∈W\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \in W.

  3. Closure under scalar multiplication - Let c∈𝔽c \in \mathbb{F} and 𝒗∈W\mathbf{v} \in W. Since WW is closed under scalar multiplication, we have c𝒗∈Wc\mathbf{v} \in W.

  4. Zero Vector - Since WW is non-empty, it contains at least one vector 𝒗\mathbf{v}. We can take c=0c = 0 and 𝒗∈W\mathbf{v} \in W, then 0𝒗=𝟎∈W0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \in W (the zero vector).

  5. Existence of Additive Inverse - Let 𝒗∈W\mathbf{v} \in W. Since WW is closed under scalar multiplication, we have −1⋅𝒗∈W-1 \cdot \mathbf{v} \in W, which is the additive inverse of 𝒗\mathbf{v}.

  6. Distributivity and Commutativity of addition - Since WW is closed under vector addition, for all 𝒖,𝒗∈W\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W, we have 𝒖+𝒗=𝒗+𝒖\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u} (commutativity) and c(𝒖+𝒗)=c𝒖+c𝒗c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v} (distributivity).

  7. Associativity of scalar multiplication - For all c,d∈𝔽c, d \in \mathbb{F} and 𝒗∈W\mathbf{v} \in W, we have c(d𝒗)=(cd)𝒗c(d\mathbf{v}) = (cd)\mathbf{v}.

Therefore, WW is a subspace of VV. Conversely if WW is a subspace of VV, then it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication by definition, and further it is non-empty and contains the zero vector. Hence proved. ◻

Example 2.2.1.5

The set of all nn-tuples of real numbers ℝn\mathbb{R}^n is a subspace of the vector space of all functions from ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝ\mathbb{R}. The zero vector is the nn-tuple of zeros, and scalar multiplication is defined as multiplying each component by a scalar.

Example 2.2.1.6

The set of all continuous functions defined on a closed interval [a,b][a, b] is a subspace of the vector space of all functions from [a,b][a, b] to ℝ\mathbb{R}. The zero vector is the zero function, and scalar multiplication is defined as multiplying the function by a real number.

Definition 2.2.1.3 (Span)

The span of a subset SS of a vector space VV, denoted span(S)\text{span}(S), is the set of all linear combinations of vectors in SS. In other words, span(S)={∑i=1nci𝒗i∣n∈ℕ,𝒗i∈S,ci∈ℝ}.\text{span}(S) = \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{v}_i \mid n \in \mathbb{N}, \mathbf{v}_i \in S, c_i \in \mathbb{R} \right\}.

Theorem 2.2.1.2 (Span of any non-empty subset of a vector space is a subspace)

Let VV be a vector space and let S⊆VS \subseteq V, S≠ϕS \neq \phi. Then span(S)\text{span}(S) is a subspace of VV.

Proof

We check all the necesary conditions for span of a non-empty subset SS of a vector space VV to be a subspace:

  1. Non-Empty - Since SS is a non-empty subset, span(S)\text{span}(S) is also non-empty by the definition of span.

  2. Closure under addition - Let 𝒖,𝒗∈span(S)\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \text{span}(S). Then there exist scalars c1,c2,…,cnc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n and d1,d2,…,dmd_1, d_2, \ldots, d_m such that: 𝒖=∑i=1nci𝒗iand𝒗=∑j=1mdj𝒘j\mathbf{u} = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{v}_i \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{v} = \sum_{j=1}^m d_j \mathbf{w}_j for some 𝒗i,𝒘j∈S\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{w}_j \in S. Then 𝒖+𝒗=∑i=1nci𝒗i+∑j=1mdj𝒘j∈span(S)\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{v}_i + \sum_{j=1}^m d_j \mathbf{w}_j \in \text{span}(S) by the definition of span.

  3. Closure under scalar multiplication - Let c∈ℝc \in \mathbb{R} and 𝒖∈span(S)\mathbf{u} \in \text{span}(S). Then there exist scalars c1,c2,…,cnc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n such that: 𝒖=∑i=1nci𝒗i\mathbf{u} = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{v}_i for some 𝒗i∈S\mathbf{v}_i \in S. Then c𝒖=c(∑i=1nci𝒗i)=∑i=1n(cci)𝒗i∈span(S)c\mathbf{u} = c\left(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{v}_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n (cc_i) \mathbf{v}_i \in \text{span}(S) by the definition of span.

Hence, all conditions are satisfied, and we can conclude that the span of any non-empty subset SS of a vector space VV is a subspace of VV. ◻

Proof

Follows directly from the fact that WW itself is a vector space with S⊆WS \subseteq W which implies span(S)\text{span}(S) is a subspace of WW from Theorem . ◻

Note 2.2.1.3

The span of a non-empty subset SS of a vector space VV is the smallest subspace of VV containing SS.

Definition 2.2.1.4 (Spanning/Generating Set)

A subset SS of a vector space VV is called a spanning/generating set if every vector in VV can be expressed as a linear combination of vectors in SS. In other words, the span of SS, denoted span(S)\text{span}(S), is equal to the entire vector space VV.

Example 2.2.1.7

A simple example of a spanning set is the set S={𝒆1,𝒆2,…,𝒆n}S = \{ \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n \}, where {𝒆1,𝒆2,…,𝒆n}\{ \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n \} is the standard basis for ℝn\mathbb{R}^n. The span of SS is the entire space ℝn\mathbb{R}^n, since any vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^n can be expressed as a linear combination of the basis vectors. We define basis shortly after.

Definition 2.2.1.5 (Linear Independence)

A subset SS of a vector space VV is called linearly independent if the only linear combination of vectors in SS that equals the zero vector is the trivial combination where all coefficients are zero. Formally, if {𝒗1,𝒗2,…,𝒗n}⊆S\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \} \subseteq S and c1𝒗1+c2𝒗2+…+cn𝒗n=𝟎c_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0} for some scalars c1,c2,…,cnc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n, then it must be the case that c1=c2=…=cn=0c_1 = c_2 = \ldots = c_n = 0.

Example 2.2.1.8

A simple example of a linearly independent set is the set S={𝒆1,𝒆2,…,𝒆n}S = \{ \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n \}, where {𝒆1,𝒆2,…,𝒆n}\{ \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n \} is the standard basis for ℝn\mathbb{R}^n. The only linear combination of these vectors that equals the zero vector is the trivial combination where all coefficients are zero. Thus, SS is linearly independent.

Definition 2.2.1.6 (Basis)

A subset BB of a vector space VV is called a basis for VV if:

  1. BB is linearly independent.

  2. The span of BB is equal to VV, i.e., span(B)=V\text{span}(B) = V.

Note that we maintain an ordering of the basis elements, which is important when working with linear operators.

Theorem 2.2.1.3 (Existence of Basis is guaranteed by existence of a spanning set)

Let VV be a vector space and let S⊆VS \subseteq V be a spanning set for VV. Then there exists a basis B⊆SB \subseteq S for VV.

Proof

If SS is linearly independent, then SS itself is a basis for VV. Otherwise, there exists a non-trivial linear combination of vectors in SS that equals the zero vector. c1𝒗1+c2𝒗2+…+cn𝒗n=𝟎c_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0} where not all cic_i are zero. Suppose ci≠0c_i \neq 0. Then - ci𝒗i=−∑j≠icj𝒗jc_i\mathbf{v}_i = -\sum_{j \neq i} c_j \mathbf{v}_j ⟹𝒗i=−∑j≠icjci𝒗j\implies \mathbf{v}_i = -\sum_{j \neq i} \frac{c_j}{c_i} \mathbf{v}_j This means that 𝒗i\mathbf{v}_i can be expressed as a linear combination of the other vectors in SS. In other words, 𝒗i\mathbf{v}_i is in the span(S)\text{span}(S). We can remove 𝒗i\mathbf{v}_i from SS to form a new set S′=S\{𝒗i}S' = S \setminus \{\mathbf{v}_i\}. Since SS is a spanning set for VV, S′S' is also a spanning set for VV. We can repeat this process until we obtain a linearly independent subset B⊆SB \subseteq S. Since BB is linearly independent and spans VV, it is a basis for VV. ◻

Definition 2.2.1.7 (Dimension)

The dimension of a vector space VV, denoted dim⁡(V)\dim(V), is the number of vectors in a basis for VV. If VV has a finite basis, we say that VV is finite-dimensional and its dimension is the cardinality of the basis set. If no finite basis exists, we say that VV is infinite-dimensional.

Theorem 2.2.1.4 (Dimension Theorem)

Any two bases for a finite-dimensional vector space have the same number of elements. In other words, the dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is well-defined. In other words, cardinality of all basis sets is the same.

Proof

Suppose two bases B1B_1 and B2B_2 of a finite-dimensional vector space VV have different cardinalities, say |B1|=n\lvert B_1 \rvert = n and |B2|=m\lvert B_2 \rvert = m, where n≠mn \neq m. Without loss of generality, assume n<mn < m. Then, since B1B_1 is a basis, it spans VV, and we can express any vector in B2B_2 as a linear combination of vectors in B1B_1.
However, since B2B_2 has more vectors than B1B_1, at least one vector in B2B_2 must be expressible as a linear combination of the others in B2B_2, contradicting the linear independence of B2B_2. Therefore, we conclude that |B1|=|B2|\lvert B_1 \rvert = \lvert B_2 \rvert, and the dimension of VV is well-defined. ◻

Theorem 2.2.1.5 (Basis Theorem)

A subset BB of a vector space VV is a basis for VV if and only if any vector in VV can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination of vectors in BB.

Proof

Suppose BB is a basis for VV. Then, by definition, BB is linearly independent and spans VV. Let 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V. Since BB spans VV, we can express 𝒗\mathbf{v} as a linear combination of vectors in BB: 𝒗=c1𝒃1+c2𝒃2+…+ck𝒃k\mathbf{v} = c_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{b}_2 + \ldots + c_k \mathbf{b}_k for some scalars c1,c2,…,ckc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k and 𝒃1,𝒃2,…,𝒃k∈B\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_k \in B. Since BB is linearly independent, the representation of 𝒗\mathbf{v} as a linear combination of vectors in BB must be unique. Formally, assume a vector 𝒗\mathbf{v} can be expressed as two different linear combinations of vectors in BB - 𝒗=c1𝒃1+c2𝒃2+…+ck𝒃k=d1𝒃1+d2𝒃2+…+dk𝒃k\mathbf{v} = c_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{b}_2 + \ldots + c_k \mathbf{b}_k = d_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + d_2 \mathbf{b}_2 + \ldots + d_k \mathbf{b}_k for some scalars c1,c2,…,ckc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k and d1,d2,…,dkd_1, d_2, \ldots, d_k. Since the basis is linearly independent, we can write - 0=(c1−d1)𝒃1+(c2−d2)𝒃2+…+(ck−dk)𝒃k0 = (c_1 - d_1) \mathbf{b}_1 + (c_2 - d_2) \mathbf{b}_2 + \ldots + (c_k - d_k) \mathbf{b}_k ⟹c1=d1,c2=d2,…,ck=dk\implies c_1 = d_1, c_2 = d_2, \ldots, c_k = d_k Hence, the representation of 𝒗\mathbf{v} as a linear combination of vectors in BB is unique.
Conversely, suppose that any vector in VV can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination of vectors in BB. Then, BB must be linearly independent; otherwise, we could find a nontrivial linear combination of vectors in BB that equals zero, contradicting the uniqueness of representation. Formally, we can write - 0=c1𝒃1+c2𝒃2+…+ck𝒃k0 = c_1 \mathbf{b}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{b}_2 + \ldots + c_k \mathbf{b}_k for some scalars c1,c2,…,ckc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k. Since the representation is unique, it follows that c1=c2=…=ck=0c_1 = c_2 = \ldots = c_k = 0. Furthermore, since any vector in VV can be expressed as a linear combination of vectors in BB, it follows that BB spans VV. Thus, BB is a basis for VV. ◻

Note 2.2.1.4

For the empty set ϕ\phi, we define span(ϕ)={𝟎}\text{span}(\phi) = \{\mathbf{0}\}, which is the trivial subspace containing only the zero vector. This is because the only linear combination of vectors in the empty set is the zero vector itself. This means that for the trivial vector space {𝟎}\{\mathbf{0}\}, the empty set ϕ\phi is a basis. Thus, the dimension of the trivial vector space is defined to be zero.

Theorem 2.2.1.6 (A linearly independent set remains linearly independent if we add a vector not in its span)

Let VV be a vector space and let S⊆VS \subseteq V be a linearly independent set. Then S∪{𝒗}S \cup \{\mathbf{v}\} is linearly independent if and only if 𝒗∉span(S)\mathbf{v} \notin \text{span}(S).

Proof

(→\rightarrow) Suppose S∪{𝒗}S \cup \{\mathbf{v}\} is linearly independent. If 𝒗∈span(S)\mathbf{v} \in \text{span}(S), then there exist scalars c1,c2,…,cnc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n such that: 𝒗=c1𝒔1+c2𝒔2+…+cn𝒔n\mathbf{v} = c_1 \mathbf{s}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{s}_2 + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{s}_n for some 𝒔1,𝒔2,…,𝒔n∈S\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_n \in S. Then we can write: 0=𝒗−(c1𝒔1+c2𝒔2+…+cn𝒔n)0 = \mathbf{v} - (c_1 \mathbf{s}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{s}_2 + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{s}_n) This is a nontrivial linear combination of vectors in S∪{𝒗}S \cup \{\mathbf{v}\} that equals zero, contradicting the linear independence of S∪{𝒗}S \cup \{\mathbf{v}\}. Therefore, 𝒗∉span(S)\mathbf{v} \notin \text{span}(S).
(←\leftarrow) Conversely, suppose 𝒗∉span(S)\mathbf{v} \notin \text{span}(S). We need to show that S∪{𝒗}S \cup \{\mathbf{v}\} is linearly independent. Assume there exist scalars c1,c2,…,cnc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n and dd such that: c1𝒔1+c2𝒔2+…+cn𝒔n+d𝒗=0c_1 \mathbf{s}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{s}_2 + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{s}_n + d\mathbf{v} = 0 for some 𝒔1,𝒔2,…,𝒔n∈S\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_n \in S. If d≠0d \neq 0, we can rearrange the equation to express 𝒗\mathbf{v} as a linear combination of vectors in SS: 𝒗=−1d(c1𝒔1+c2𝒔2+…+cn𝒔n)\mathbf{v} = -\frac{1}{d}(c_1 \mathbf{s}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{s}_2 + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{s}_n) This contradicts the assumption that 𝒗∉span(S)\mathbf{v} \notin \text{span}(S). Therefore, d=0d = 0, and since SS is linearly independent, it follows that c1=c2=…=cn=0c_1 = c_2 = \ldots = c_n = 0. Thus, S∪{𝒗}S \cup \{\mathbf{v}\} is linearly independent. ◻

Theorem 2.2.1.7 (|L|≤|S||L| \leq |S| for any linearly independent set LL and spanning set SS of a finite-dimensional vector space VV)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space. If L⊆VL \subseteq V is a linearly independent set and S⊆VS \subseteq V is a spanning set, then |L|≤|S|\lvert L \rvert \leq \lvert S \rvert.

Proof

Let LL be a linearly independent set and SS be a spanning set of a finite-dimensional vector space VV. Let |L|=m|L| = m and |S|=n|S| = n. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that m>nm > n. Since SS spans VV, every vector in LL can be expressed as a linear combination of vectors in SS. This means that we can write each vector in LL as: 𝒍i=∑j=1ncij𝒔j\mathbf{l}_i = \sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij} \mathbf{s}_j for some scalars cijc_{ij} and vectors 𝒔j∈S\mathbf{s}_j \in S. Since m>nm > n, we have more vectors in LL than in SS. By the pigeonhole principle, at least one vector in SS must be used in the linear combinations of at least two different vectors in LL. This implies that there exists a nontrivial linear combination of vectors in LL that equals zero, contradicting the linear independence of LL. Therefore, we conclude that m≤nm \leq n, or |L|≤|S|\lvert L \rvert \leq \lvert S \rvert. ◻

Theorem 2.2.1.8 (Extending a linearly independent set to a basis)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space and let L⊆VL \subseteq V be a linearly independent set. Then we can extend LL to a basis BB for VV, i.e., there exists a basis BB for VV such that L⊆BL \subseteq B.

Proof

Let L={𝒍1,𝒍2,…,𝒍m}L = \{\mathbf{l}_1, \mathbf{l}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{l}_m\} be a linearly independent set in a finite-dimensional vector space VV. If LL already spans VV, then LL is a basis for VV. Otherwise, there exists a vector 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V that is not in the span of LL. We can add this vector to LL to form a new set L′=L∪{𝒗}L' = L \cup \{\mathbf{v}\}. By the previous theorem, since 𝒗∉span(L)\mathbf{v} \notin \text{span}(L), the set L′L' is also linearly independent. We can repeat this process, adding vectors not in the span of the current set until we obtain a set that spans VV. Since VV is finite-dimensional, this process must terminate after a finite number of steps. The resulting set is a basis for VV that contains the original linearly independent set LL. ◻

2.3 Exercises

2.3.1 Selected Exercises from Artin’s Algebra

2.3.1.1 Groups: Laws of Composition

Exercise 2.3.1.1

Let SS be a set. Prove that the law of composition *:S×S→S*: S \times S \to S, a*b=aa * b = a is associative. For which sets does this law have an identity element?

Proof

To show that the law of composition *:S×S→S*: S \times S \to S defined by a*b=aa * b = a is associative, we need to verify that for all a,b,c∈Sa, b, c \in S, (a*b)*c=a*(b*c)(a * b) * c = a * (b * c). We compute both sides for arbitrary elements a,b,c∈Sa, b, c \in S: (a*b)*c=a*c=a(a * b) * c = a * c = a and a*(b*c)=a*b=aa * (b * c) = a * b = a Since both sides equal aa, the law is associative.
Now, for the identity element, we need an element e∈Se \in S such that for all a∈Sa \in S, e*a=ae * a = a and a*e=aa * e = a. The only candidate for such an identity element is any arbitrary element of SS, since e*a=ee * a = e for all aa. Thus, there is no unique identity element unless SS has exactly one element. ◻

Exercise 2.3.1.2

Let ℕ\mathbb{N} be the set of natural numbers. Show that the map defined by f:ℕ→ℕf: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}, f(n)=n+1f(n) = n + 1 is a law of composition on ℕ\mathbb{N}. Show also that it has no right inverse and infinitely many left inverses.

Proof

The map f:ℕ→ℕf: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} defined by f(n)=n+1f(n) = n + 1 is a law of composition because it takes any natural number nn and maps it to another natural number n+1n + 1. This operation is well-defined on ℕ\mathbb{N}, as the output is always a natural number (can be shown using induction)
To show that ff has no right inverse, we assume there exists a function g:ℕ→ℕg: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} such that f(g(n))=nf(g(n)) = n for all n∈ℕn \in \mathbb{N}. This would imply g(n)=n−1g(n) = n - 1, which is not defined for n=1n = 1. Hence, no right inverse exists.
For left inverses, consider the function h:ℕ→ℕh: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} defined by h(n)=n−1h(n) = n - 1 for all n>1n > 1 and h(1)=1h(1) = 1. This function satisfies h(f(n))=h(n+1)=nh(f(n)) = h(n + 1) = n, thus providing infinitely many left inverses. ◻

2.3.1.2 Groups and Subgroups

Exercise 2.3.1.3

Let SS be a set with an associative law of composition ** and with an identity element ee. Prove that the subset of consisting of invertible elements of SS is a group under the law of composition **.

Proof

Let SS be a set with an associative law of composition ** and an identity element ee. We define the subset H⊆SH \subseteq S consisting of all invertible elements of SS, i.e., elements a∈Sa \in S such that there exists an element b∈Sb \in S with a*b=b*a=ea * b = b * a = e. We need to show that HH is a group under the law of composition **.

To show that HH is a group, we need to verify the group properties:

  1. Closure: Let a,b∈Ha, b \in H. Since both are invertible, there exist c,d∈Sc, d \in S such that a*c=c*a=ea * c = c * a = e and b*d=d*b=eb * d = d * b = e. We need to show that a*b∈Ha * b \in H. Consider the element d*cd * c. We have: (a*b)*(d*c)=a*(b*(d*c))=a*((b*d)*c)=a*(e*c)=a*c=e(a * b) * (d * c) = a * (b * (d * c)) = a * ((b * d) * c) = a * (e * c) = a * c = e Similarly, we can show that (d*c)*(a*b)=e(d * c) * (a * b) = e. Thus, a*ba * b is invertible and belongs to SS [since ** is a law of composition on SS] which implies that a*b∈Ha * b \in H.

  2. Associativity: Since the law of composition on SS is associative, it follows that for all a,b,c∈Ha, b, c \in H, (a*b)*c=a*(b*c)(a * b) * c = a * (b * c).

  3. Identity Element: The identity element ee is in HH since it is invertible with itself as its inverse.

  4. Inverse Element: For every element a∈Ha \in H, there exists an inverse element in HH, which is defined by the property of invertibility. Specifically, if aa has an inverse bb, then both are in HH.

Therefore, the subset of invertible elements of SS forms a group under the law of composition **. ◻

Exercise 2.3.1.4

Is the set of of 2×22\times 2 matrices of the form (a000)\begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} where a∈ℝa \in \mathbb{R} a subgroup of GL(2,ℝ)GL(2, \mathbb{R})? Justify your answer.

Proof

No, the set of matrices of the form (a000)\begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} where a∈ℝa \in \mathbb{R} is not a subgroup of GL(2,ℝ)GL(2, \mathbb{R}). To be a subgroup, it must satisfy the group properties under matrix multiplication.

  1. Closure: Let A=(a000)A = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and B=(b000)B = \begin{pmatrix} b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} be two matrices in the set. Their product is given by: A*B=(a000)*(b000)=(ab000)A * B = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} * \begin{pmatrix} b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ab & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} Since ab∈ℝab \in \mathbb{R}, the product A*BA * B is also of the same form and belongs to the set.

  2. Identity Element: The identity element in GL(2,ℝ)GL(2, \mathbb{R}) is the matrix I=(1001)I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. However, this matrix is not of the form (a000)\begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, so the identity element is not in the set.

  3. Inverse Element: For a matrix A=(a000)A = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} to have an inverse in the set, there must exist a matrix B=(b000)B = \begin{pmatrix} b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} such that A*B=IA * B = I. By properties of the inverses of matrices and determinants, we can determine that since the determinant of AA is 00 (as the second row and column are zero), it does not have an inverse in GL(2,ℝ)GL(2, \mathbb{R}). Therefore, not all elements in the set have inverses in the set.

 ◻

Exercise 2.3.1.5

Let GG be a group with an identity element ee. Show that any subgroup HH of GG is a group with the same unique identity element ee.

Proof

We first prove that the identity element ee is unique in the group GG. Suppose there are two identity elements e1e_1 and e2e_2 in GG. By the definition of an identity element, we have: e1*e2=e2(since e1 is an identity)e_1 * e_2 = e_2 \quad \text{(since $e_1$ is an identity)} and similarly, e2*e1=e1(since e2 is an identity)e_2 * e_1 = e_1 \quad \text{(since $e_2$ is an identity)} Therefore, by the law of cancellation and commutativity of the identity element, we have: e1=e2e_1 = e_2 This shows that the identity element is unique.

Now, since HH is a subgroup of GG, it inherits the group structure from GG. In particular, the identity element ee of GG is also the identity element of HH. To see this, let h∈Hh \in H. Then we have: h*e=h(since e is an identity in G)h * e = h \quad \text{(since $e$ is an identity in $G$)} and e*h=h(since e is an identity in G)e * h = h \quad \text{(since $e$ is an identity in $G$)} Thus, ee acts as the identity element in HH as well.

Therefore, any subgroup HH of GG is a group with the same unique identity element ee. [This works because the identity element is unique in any group and every subgroup inherits the group structure and must have an identity element for the same group operation.] ◻

2.3.1.3 Vector Spaces

Exercise 2.3.1.6

Prove that the scalar product of a vector with the zero vector is zero, i.e., for any vector 𝒗∈V\mathbf{v} \in V and scalar c∈Fc \in F, c𝟎=𝟎c\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}.

Proof

Suppose the contrary that there exists a vector 𝒗∈V,𝒗≠𝟎\mathbf{v} \in V, \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0} and a scalar c∈Fc \in F such that c𝟎=𝒗c\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v}. Then we can write, by distributive properties of scalar multiplication over vector addition - c𝟎=c(𝟎+𝟎)=c𝟎+c𝟎=𝒗c\mathbf{0} = c(\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0}) = c\mathbf{0} + c\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v} ⟹2c𝟎=𝒗\implies 2c\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v} But we assumed that 𝒗=c𝟎\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{0}, which implies that 2𝒗=𝒗2\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}. This is a contradiction if 𝒗≠𝟎\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}. Hence proved. ◻

Exercise 2.3.1.7

Prove that if ww is an element of a subspace WW of a vector space VV, then −w-w is also an element of WW.

Proof

Let WW be a subspace of a vector space VV, and let w∈Ww \in W. By the definition of a subspace, WW is closed under scalar multiplication and contains the zero vector. Since w∈Ww \in W, we can consider the scalar multiplication of ww by −1-1: −w=(−1)w-w = (-1)w Since WW is closed under scalar multiplication, it follows that −w∈W-w \in W. Therefore, if ww is an element of a subspace WW, then its additive inverse −w-w is also an element of WW. ◻

Exercise 2.3.1.8

Prove that the set of all n×nn \times n matrices over a field FF forms a vector space over FF. Further show which of the following sets are subspaces of this vector space:

  1. The set of all symmetric matrices.

  2. The set of all invertible matrices.

  3. The set of all upper triangular matrices.

Proof

To show that the set of all n×nn \times n matrices over a field FF, denoted as Mn(F)M_n(F), forms a vector space over FF, we need to verify the vector space axioms:

  1. Closure under Addition: For any two matrices A,B∈Mn(F)A, B \in M_n(F), their sum A+BA + B is also an n×nn \times n matrix, hence A+B∈Mn(F)A + B \in M_n(F).

  2. Associativity of Addition: Matrix addition is associative, i.e., (A+B)+C=A+(B+C)(A + B) + C = A + (B + C) for all A,B,C∈Mn(F)A, B, C \in M_n(F).

  3. Commutativity of Addition: Matrix addition is commutative, i.e., A+B=B+AA + B = B + A for all A,B∈Mn(F)A, B \in M_n(F).

  4. Existence of Zero Vector: The zero matrix 0n×n0_{n \times n} serves as the additive identity in Mn(F)M_n(F).

  5. Existence of Additive Inverses: For any matrix A∈Mn(F)A \in M_n(F), its additive inverse is given by −A-A, which is also an n×nn \times n matrix.

  6. Closure under Scalar Multiplication: For any scalar α∈F\alpha \in F and matrix A∈Mn(F)A \in M_n(F), the product αA\alpha A is also an n×nn \times n matrix.

  7. Distributive Property: Scalar multiplication distributes over matrix addition and scalar addition, by definition.

  8. Associativity of Scalar Multiplication: Scalar multiplication is associative with respect to field multiplication.

Thus, Mn(F)M_n(F) is a vector space over the field FF. Now we check which of the following sets are subspaces of this vector space:

  1. The set of all symmetric matrices: A matrix AA is symmetric if AT=AA^T = A. This set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. If A,BA, B are symmetric matrices, then (A+B)T=AT+BT=A+B(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T = A + B, and for any scalar α\alpha, (αA)T=αA(\alpha A)^T = \alpha A. The zero matrix is symmetric, and the additive inverse of a symmetric matrix is also symmetric. Therefore, the set of all symmetric matrices is a subspace of Mn(F)M_n(F).

  2. The set of all invertible matrices: This set is not a subspace because it is not closed under addition. For example, the matrices (1001)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and (−100−1)\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} are both invertible, but their sum (0000)\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is not invertible. Therefore, the set of all invertible matrices is not a subspace of Mn(F)M_n(F). Further the zero matrix is not included in the set of all invertible matrices.

  3. The set of all upper triangular matrices: A matrix is upper triangular if all entries below the main diagonal are zero. This set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. If AA and BB are upper triangular matrices, then (A+B)(A + B) is also upper triangular, and for any scalar α\alpha, (αA)(\alpha A) is also upper triangular. The zero matrix is upper triangular, and the additive inverse of an upper triangular matrix is also upper triangular. Therefore, the set of all upper triangular matrices is a subspace of Mn(F)M_n(F).

Hence proved. ◻

Exercise 2.3.1.9

Let VV be a vector space over an infinite field FF. Prove that VV is not a union of finitely many proper subspaces.

Proof

Let us assume the contrapositive statement. Let us assume we can express the vector space VV as the union of finitely many proper subspaces. Let WiW_i be the ithi^{th} proper subspace of VV we consider. Then, for some n∈ℕn \in \mathbb{N}, we can write - V=⋃i=1nWiV = \bigcup_{i = 1}^{n} W_i By the definition of a proper subspace we have that - ∀i,∃𝒗i∈V:𝒗i∉Wi\forall i, \exists \mathbf{v}_i \in V: \mathbf{v}_i \notin W_i Consider the set of all such vectors 𝒗i\mathbf{v}_i for i=1,2,…,ni = 1, 2, \ldots, n. This set is non-empty since for each ii, we can find a vector 𝒗i\mathbf{v}_i not in the corresponding subspace WiW_i. Let S={𝒗1,𝒗2,…,𝒗n}S = \{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\}. Now, since FF is an infinite field, we can find a linear combination of the vectors in SS that is not in the span of the ⋃i=1nWi\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}W_i. This contradicts the assumption that VV is the union of the WiW_i. Therefore, our initial assumption must be false, and VV cannot be expressed as a union of finitely many proper subspaces. ◻

2.3.2 Selected exercises from Hoffman Kunze

2.3.2.1 Subspaces

Exercise 2.3.2.1

Let W1W_1 and W2W_2 be two subspaces of a vector space VV such that the union of the two is also a subspace. Prove that one of W1W_1 and W2W_2 is contained in the other.

Proof

We need to show that, WLOG, W1⊆W2W_1 \subseteq W_2. Suppose the contrary that W1⊈W2W_1 \nsubseteq W_2 and W2⊈W1W_2 \nsubseteq W_1. Then, there exist vectors 𝒗𝟏∈W1\mathbf{v_1} \in W_1 and 𝒗𝟐∈W2\mathbf{v_2} \in W_2 such that 𝒗𝟏∉W2\mathbf{v_1} \notin W_2 and 𝒗𝟐∉W1\mathbf{v_2} \notin W_1. Consider the vector 𝒗𝟏+𝒗𝟐\mathbf{v_1} + \mathbf{v_2}. Since W1∪W2W_1 \cup W_2 is a subspace, it must be closed under addition. Therefore, we have 𝒗𝟏+𝒗𝟐∈W1∪W2\mathbf{v_1} + \mathbf{v_2} \in W_1 \cup W_2. However, 𝒗𝟏+𝒗𝟐\mathbf{v_1} + \mathbf{v_2} cannot be in W2W_2 because 𝒗𝟏∉W2\mathbf{v_1} \notin W_2. Thus, 𝒗𝟏+𝒗𝟐\mathbf{v_1} + \mathbf{v_2} must be in W1W_1. Similarly, since 𝒗𝟐∉W1\mathbf{v_2} \notin W_1, we can conclude that 𝒗𝟏+𝒗𝟐∈W2\mathbf{v_1} + \mathbf{v_2} \in W_2. This is a contradiction. Hence, one of W1W_1 or W2W_2 must be contained in the other. ◻

Exercise 2.3.2.2

Let VV be the vector space of all functions from ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝ\mathbb{R}. Let the set of all even functions be VeV_e and set of all odd functions be VoV_o. Show the following -

  1. VeV_e and VoV_o are subspaces of VV

  2. Ve∩Vo={0}V_e \cap V_o = \{0\}

  3. V=Ve⊕VoV = V_e \oplus V_o

Proof

We prove each property in turn.

  1. To show that VeV_e is a subspace of VV, we need to verify that it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. The zero function is included in both sets of odd functions and even functions by definition and we can find examples of both to show that both are non-empty. Now -
    Let f,g∈Vef, g \in V_e. Then, for all x∈ℝx \in \mathbb{R}, we have f(x)=f(−x)f(x) = f(-x) and g(x)=g(−x)g(x) = g(-x). Therefore, for all x∈ℝx \in \mathbb{R}: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)=f(−x)+g(−x)=(f+g)(−x)(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) = f(-x) + g(-x) = (f + g)(-x) Thus, f+g∈Vef + g \in V_e. Now, let c∈ℝc \in \mathbb{R} and f∈Vef \in V_e. Then, for all x∈ℝx \in \mathbb{R}: (cf)(x)=cf(x)=cf(−x)=(cf)(−x)(cf)(x) = c f(x) = c f(-x) = (cf)(-x) Hence, cf∈Vecf \in V_e. Therefore, VeV_e is a subspace of VV. A similar argument shows that VoV_o is also a subspace of VV.

  2. To show that Ve∩Vo={0}V_e \cap V_o = \{0\}, let f∈Ve∩Vof \in V_e \cap V_o. Then, for all x∈ℝx \in \mathbb{R}: f(x)=f(−x)(even)f(x) = f(-x) \quad \text{(even)} f(x)=−f(−x)(odd)f(x) = -f(-x) \quad \text{(odd)} Combining these two equations, we get: f(x)=−f(x)f(x) = -f(x) This implies that f(x)=0f(x) = 0 for all x∈ℝx \in \mathbb{R}. Hence, f=0f = 0, and we conclude that Ve∩Vo={0}V_e \cap V_o = \{0\}.

  3. To show that V=Ve⊕VoV = V_e \oplus V_o, we need to show that every function f∈Vf \in V can be uniquely expressed as the sum of an even function and an odd function. We can define: fe(x)=f(x)+f(−x)2(even part)f_e(x) = \frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2} \quad \text{(even part)} fo(x)=f(x)−f(−x)2(odd part)f_o(x) = \frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2} \quad \text{(odd part)} It is straightforward to verify that fe∈Vef_e \in V_e and fo∈Vof_o \in V_o. Moreover, we have: f(x)=fe(x)+fo(x)f(x) = f_e(x) + f_o(x) To show uniqueness, suppose there exist ge∈Veg_e \in V_e and go∈Vog_o \in V_o such that: f=ge+gof = g_e + g_o Then, by the properties of even and odd functions, we can show that ge=feg_e = f_e and go=fog_o = f_o. Thus, we conclude that V=Ve⊕VoV = V_e \oplus V_o.

 ◻

2.3.2.2 Basis and Dimension

Exercise 2.3.2.3

Show that if two vectors are linearly dependent, then one of them is a scalar multiple of the other.

Proof

Let 𝒗𝟏\mathbf{v_1} and 𝒗𝟐\mathbf{v_2} be two linearly dependent vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^n. By definition of linear dependence, there exist scalars c1c_1 and c2c_2, not both zero, such that: c1𝒗𝟏+c2𝒗𝟐=𝟎c_1 \mathbf{v_1} + c_2 \mathbf{v_2} = \mathbf{0} Without loss of generality, assume c2≠0c_2 \neq 0. Then we can solve for 𝒗𝟐\mathbf{v_2}: 𝒗𝟐=−c1c2𝒗𝟏\mathbf{v_2} = -\frac{c_1}{c_2} \mathbf{v_1} This shows that 𝒗𝟐\mathbf{v_2} is a scalar multiple of 𝒗𝟏\mathbf{v_1}. The case where c1≠0c_1 \neq 0 is similar. Hence, we conclude that if two vectors are linearly dependent, then one of them is a scalar multiple of the other. ◻

Exercise 2.3.2.4

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF. Suppose there are a finite number of vectors 𝒗𝟏,𝒗𝟐,…,𝒗𝒏∈V\mathbf{v_1}, \mathbf{v_2}, \ldots, \mathbf{v_n} \in V such that: span(𝒗𝟏,𝒗𝟐,…,𝒗𝒏)=V\text{span}(\mathbf{v_1}, \mathbf{v_2}, \ldots, \mathbf{v_n}) = V. Show that VV is finite-dimensional even if the set is not a basis.

Proof

Suppose that the set has a vector that can be written as a linear combination of the others. Then, we can remove that vector from the set without changing the span. We can prove this statement - let 𝒗𝒌\mathbf{v_k} be such a vector. Then, we can write: 𝒗𝒌=c1𝒗𝟏+c2𝒗𝟐+…+ck−1𝒗𝒌−𝟏+ck+1𝒗𝒌+𝟏+…+cn𝒗𝒏\mathbf{v_k} = c_1 \mathbf{v_1} + c_2 \mathbf{v_2} + \ldots + c_{k-1} \mathbf{v_{k-1}} + c_{k+1} \mathbf{v_{k+1}} + \ldots + c_n \mathbf{v_n} for some scalars c1,c2,…,ck−1,ck+1,…,cnc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_{k-1}, c_{k+1}, \ldots, c_n. This shows that 𝒗𝒌\mathbf{v_k} can be expressed as a linear combination of the other vectors in the set. Suppose we remove 𝒗𝒌\mathbf{v_k} from the set, we still have: span(𝒗𝟏,𝒗𝟐,…,𝒗𝒌−𝟏,𝒗𝒌+𝟏,…,𝒗𝒏)=V\text{span}(\mathbf{v_1}, \mathbf{v_2}, \ldots, \mathbf{v_{k-1}}, \mathbf{v_{k+1}}, \ldots, \mathbf{v_n}) = V since 𝒗𝒌\mathbf{v_k} can be expressed as a linear combination of the other vectors (this means that 𝒗𝒌\mathbf{v_k} can be excluded from the spanning set and it would still span VV since 𝒗𝒌∈V\mathbf{v_k} \in V and it is also included in the span of the other vectors since it can be expressed as a linear combination of said vectors). We can repeat this process until we obtain a set of vectors that are linearly independent and still span VV. This process will terminate after a finite number of steps because we started with a finite set of vectors (in fact an algorithm can be designed for this purpose). Thus, we can find a finite basis (a linearly independent ordered set of vectors which spans VV) for VV, which implies that VV is finite-dimensional. Therefore, if there are a finite number of vectors such that their span equals VV, we conclude that VV is finite-dimensional. ◻

Exercise 2.3.2.5

Let VV be the set of real numbers. Regard VV as a vector field over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, with the usual addition and multiplication. Show that VV is not finite-dimensional over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Proof

Suppose the contrary that there exists a finite basis {𝒗𝟏,𝒗𝟐,…,𝒗𝒏}\{ \mathbf{v_1}, \mathbf{v_2}, \ldots, \mathbf{v_n} \} for VV over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.
