    Now, for any ii such that 1≤i≤k1 \leq i \leq k, we compute B(uk+1,ui)B(u_{k+1}, u_i): B(uk+1,ui)=B(vk+1−∑j=1kB(vk+1,uj)B(uj,uj)uj,ui)=B(vk+1,ui)−∑j=1kB(vk+1,uj)B(uj,uj)B(uj,ui)\begin{aligned} B(u_{k+1}, u_i) &= B\left(v_{k+1} - \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{B(v_{k+1}, u_j)}{B(u_j, u_j)} u_j, u_i\right) \\ &= B(v_{k+1}, u_i) - \sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{B(v_{k+1}, u_j)}{B(u_j, u_j)} B(u_j, u_i) \end{aligned}

    Since {u1,u2,…,uk}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k\} is an orthogonal set by the inductive hypothesis, we have B(uj,ui)=0B(u_j, u_i) = 0 for all j≠ij \neq i. Therefore, the sum reduces to: B(uk+1,ui)=B(vk+1,ui)−B(vk+1,ui)B(ui,ui)B(ui,ui)B(u_{k+1}, u_i) = B(v_{k+1}, u_i) - \frac{B(v_{k+1}, u_i)}{B(u_i, u_i)} B(u_i, u_i)

    Simplifying this expression gives: B(uk+1,ui)=B(vk+1,ui)−B(vk+1,ui)=0B(u_{k+1}, u_i) = B(v_{k+1}, u_i) - B(v_{k+1}, u_i) = 0 Thus, uk+1u_{k+1} is orthogonal to each of the previous vectors u1,u2,…,uku_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k.

By induction, we conclude that the set {u1,u2,…,un}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n\} is orthogonal with respect to the bilinear form BB. ◻

4.3.3 Skew-Symmetric Bilinear Forms

Definition 4.3.3.1 (Skew-Symmetric Bilinear Form)

A bilinear form B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F on a vector space VV over a field FF is called skew-symmetric (or antisymmetric) if for all vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V, the following condition holds: B(u,v)=−B(v,u)B(u, v) = -B(v, u)

Example 4.3.3.1

Let V=ℝ2V = \mathbb{R}^2 be the vector space of all ordered pairs of real numbers. Define a bilinear form B:V×V→ℝB: V \times V \to \mathbb{R} by: B((x1,y1),(x2,y2))=x1y2−y1x2B((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = x_1y_2 - y_1x_2 We can verify that BB is skew-symmetric: B((x1,y1),(x2,y2))=x1y2−y1x2B((x2,y2),(x1,y1))=x2y1−y2x1=−(x1y2−y1x2)=−B((x1,y1),(x2,y2))\begin{aligned} B((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) &= x_1y_2 - y_1x_2 \\ B((x_2, y_2), (x_1, y_1)) &= x_2y_1 - y_2x_1 \\ &= -(x_1y_2 - y_1x_2) \\ &= -B((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) \end{aligned} Thus, B((x1,y1),(x2,y2))=−B((x2,y2),(x1,y1))B((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = -B((x_2, y_2), (x_1, y_1)), confirming that BB is a skew-symmetric bilinear form.

4.3.4 Hermitian Forms

We now extend the concept of bilinear forms to complex vector spaces, leading to the definition of Hermitian forms. First we define the complex conjugate.

Definition 4.3.4.1 (Complex Conjugate)

The complex conjugate of a complex number z=a+biz = a + bi, where a,b∈ℝa, b \in \mathbb{R} and ii is the imaginary unit, is defined as: z¯=a−bi\overline{z} = a - bi

We also define the conjugate transpose of a matrix.

Definition 4.3.4.2 (Conjugate Transpose)

Let A=[aij]A = [a_{ij}] be a complex matrix. The conjugate transpose of AA, denoted by A*A^*, is obtained by taking the transpose of AA and then taking the complex conjugate of each entry. Formally, (A*)ij=aji¯(A^*)_{ij} = \overline{a_{ji}}

Now we are ready to define Hermitian forms.

Definition 4.3.4.3 (Hermitian Form)

A Hermitian form on a complex vector space VV is a function H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} that satisfies the following properties for all vectors u,v,w∈Vu, v, w \in V and all scalars c∈𝒞c \in \mathcal{C}:

  1. Conjugate Symmetry: H(u,v)=H(v,u)¯H(u, v) = \overline{H(v, u)}

  2. Linearity in the First Argument: H(cu+v,w)=cH(u,w)+H(v,w)H(cu + v, w) = cH(u, w) + H(v, w)

  3. Linearity in the Second Argument: H(u,cv+w)=c¯H(u,v)+H(u,w)H(u, cv + w) = \overline{c}H(u, v) + H(u, w)

  4. Positive Definiteness: H(v,v)>0H(v, v) > 0 for all non-zero vectors v∈Vv \in V

The standard Hermitian form on 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^n is given by: H(u,v)=u*v=∑i=1nui¯viH(u, v) = u^* v = \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{u_i} v_i where u=(u1,u2,…,un)u = (u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n) and v=(v1,v2,…,vn)v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) are vectors in 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^n, and u*u^* denotes the conjugate transpose of uu.
We further define the Adjoint of a Linear Operator with respect to a Hermitian Form.

Definition 4.3.4.4 (Adjoint of a Linear Operator)

We define the adjoint of a matrix first. Let A∈Mn(𝒞)A \in M_n(\mathcal{C}). The adjoint of AA, denoted by A*A^*, is defined as the conjugate transpose of AA. That is, (A*)ij=aji¯(A^*)_{ij} = \overline{a_{ji}} In particular, (AB)*=B*A*(AB)^* = B^* A^*.

Definition 4.3.4.5 (Self Adjoint or Hermitian Operator)

A linear operator T:V→VT: V \to V on a complex vector space VV is called Hermitian if T=T*T = T^*, where T*T^* is the adjoint of TT.

We now define the gram matrix of a Hermitian form.

Definition 4.3.4.6 (Gram Matrix of a Hermitian Form)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} be a Hermitian form on VV. If {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} is a basis for VV, then the Gram matrix GG of the Hermitian form HH with respect to the basis {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} is defined as the n×nn \times n matrix whose entries are given by: Gij=H(vi,vj)for 1≤i,j≤nG_{ij} = H(v_i, v_j) \quad \text{for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n

Theorem 4.3.4.1 (Gram Matrix of a Hermitian Form is Hermitian)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} be a Hermitian form on VV. If {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} is a basis for VV, then the Gram matrix GG of the Hermitian form HH with respect to the basis {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} is a Hermitian matrix. That is, Gij=Gji¯for all 1≤i,j≤nG_{ij} = \overline{G_{ji}} \quad \text{for all }1 \leq i, j \leq n

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} be a Hermitian form on VV. Let {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} be a basis for VV, and let GG be the Gram matrix of the Hermitian form HH with respect to this basis. The entries of the Gram matrix are given by: Gij=H(vi,vj)for 1≤i,j≤nG_{ij} = H(v_i, v_j) \quad \text{for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n Since HH is Hermitian, we have: Gij=H(vi,vj)=H(vj,vi)¯=Gji¯\begin{aligned} G_{ij} &= H(v_i, v_j) \\ &= \overline{H(v_j, v_i)} \\ &= \overline{G_{ji}} \end{aligned} Thus, Gij=Gji¯G_{ij} = \overline{G_{ji}} for all 1≤i,j≤n1 \leq i, j \leq n, confirming that the Gram matrix GG is Hermitian. ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.2 (Change of Basis for Hermitian Form Gram Matrix)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} be a Hermitian form on VV. Let {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} and {w1,w2,…,wn}\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\} be two bases for VV, and let GvG_v and GwG_w be the Gram matrices of the Hermitian form HH with respect to the bases {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} and {w1,w2,…,wn}\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\}, respectively. If PP is the change of basis matrix from the basis {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} to the basis {w1,w2,…,wn}\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\}, then the Gram matrices are related by: Gw=P*GvPG_w = P^* G_v P

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} be a Hermitian form on VV. Let {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} and {w1,w2,…,wn}\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\} be two bases for VV, and let GvG_v and GwG_w be the Gram matrices of the Hermitian form HH with respect to the bases {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} and {w1,w2,…,wn}\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\}, respectively. Let PP be the change of basis matrix from the basis {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} to the basis {w1,w2,…,wn}\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\}. Then, for any vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V, we can express them in terms of the two bases: u=∑i=1naivi=∑j=1nbjwjv=∑i=1ncivi=∑j=1ndjwj\begin{aligned} u &= \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n b_j w_j \\ v &= \sum_{i=1}^n c_i v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n d_j w_j \end{aligned} where ai,bj,ci,dj∈𝒞a_i, b_j, c_i, d_j \in \mathcal{C}. The coefficients are related by the change of basis matrix PP: (b1b2⋮bn)=P(a1a2⋮an),(d1d2⋮dn)=P(c1c2⋮cn)\begin{pmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ \vdots \\ b_n \end{pmatrix} = P \begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \\ \vdots \\ a_n \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ \vdots \\ d_n \end{pmatrix} = P \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{pmatrix} Now, we compute H(u,v)H(u, v) using both bases: H(u,v)=(a1a2…an)Gv(c1c2⋮cn)=(b1b2…bn)Gw(d1d2⋮dn)\begin{aligned} H(u, v) &= \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & \ldots & a_n \end{pmatrix} G_v \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} b_1 & b_2 & \ldots & b_n \end{pmatrix} G_w \begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ \vdots \\ d_n \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} Substituting the expressions for bjb_j and djd_j in terms of aia_i and cic_i, we get: H(u,v)=(a1a2…an)P*GwP(c1c2⋮cn)\begin{aligned} H(u, v) &= \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & \ldots & a_n \end{pmatrix} P^* G_w P \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} Since this holds for all vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V, we conclude that: Gw=P*GvPG_w = P^* G_v P ◻

Definition 4.3.4.7 (Inner Product)

For a real vector space VV, an inner product is a symmetric bilinear form B:V×V→ℝB: V \times V \to \mathbb{R} that is also positive definite. That is, for all non-zero vectors v∈Vv \in V, we have: B(v,v)>0B(v, v) > 0 For a complex vector space VV, an inner product is a Hermitian form H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C} that is also positive definite. That is, for all non-zero vectors v∈Vv \in V, we have: H(v,v)>0H(v, v) > 0

Definition 4.3.4.8 (Euclidean Space)

A Euclidean space is a finite-dimensional real vector space VV equipped with an inner product B:V×V→ℝB: V \times V \to \mathbb{R}. The inner product induces a norm on the space, defined by: ∥v∥=B(v,v)\|v\| = \sqrt{B(v, v)}

Definition 4.3.4.9 (Hermitian Space)

A Hermitian space is a finite-dimensional complex vector space VV equipped with an inner product H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C}. The inner product induces a norm on the space, defined by: ∥v∥=H(v,v)\|v\| = \sqrt{H(v, v)}

Theorem 4.3.4.3 (Eigenvalues of Hermitian Matrix are Real)

Let A∈Mn(𝒞)A \in M_n(\mathcal{C}) be a Hermitian matrix, i.e., A=A*A = A^*. Then, all eigenvalues of AA are real numbers.

Proof

Let A∈Mn(𝒞)A \in M_n(\mathcal{C}) be a Hermitian matrix, i.e., A=A*A = A^*. Let λ∈𝒞\lambda \in \mathcal{C} be an eigenvalue of AA, and let v∈𝒞nv \in \mathcal{C}^n be a corresponding eigenvector, i.e., Av=λvAv = \lambda v with v≠0v \neq 0. We want to show that λ\lambda is a real number.
Consider the inner product of AvAv with vv: ⟨Av,v⟩=⟨λv,v⟩=λ⟨v,v⟩\begin{aligned} \langle Av, v \rangle &= \langle \lambda v, v \rangle \\ &= \lambda \langle v, v \rangle \end{aligned} Since AA is Hermitian, we have: ⟨Av,v⟩=⟨v,A*v⟩=⟨v,Av⟩=⟨v,λv⟩=λ¯⟨v,v⟩\begin{aligned} \langle Av, v \rangle &= \langle v, A^* v \rangle \\ &= \langle v, Av \rangle \\ &= \langle v, \lambda v \rangle \\ &= \overline{\lambda} \langle v, v \rangle \end{aligned} Equating the two expressions for ⟨Av,v⟩\langle Av, v \rangle, we get: λ⟨v,v⟩=λ¯⟨v,v⟩\lambda \langle v, v \rangle = \overline{\lambda} \langle v, v \rangle Since ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v, v \rangle > 0 (as v≠0v \neq 0), we can divide both sides by ⟨v,v⟩\langle v, v \rangle to obtain: λ=λ¯\lambda = \overline{\lambda} This shows that λ\lambda is equal to its complex conjugate, which means λ\lambda is a real number. ◻

Definition 4.3.4.10 (Orthogonal Matrix)

Let A∈Mn×n(ℝ)A \in M_{n\times n}(\mathbb{R}). The matrix AA is called orthogonal if its column vectors form an orthonormal basis of ℝn\mathbb{R}^n with respect to the standard inner product. Equivalently, AA is orthogonal if: ATA=AAT=InA^T A = AA^T = I_n where ATA^T is the transpose of AA and InI_n is the n×nn \times n identity matrix.

Definition 4.3.4.11 (Unitary Matrix)

Let A∈Mn×n(𝒞)A \in M_{n\times n}(\mathcal{C}). The matrix AA is called unitary if its column vectors form an orthonormal basis of 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^n with respect to the standard inner product. Equivalently, AA is unitary if: A*A=AA*=InA^* A = AA^* = I_n where A*A^* is the conjugate transpose of AA and InI_n is the n×nn \times n identity matrix.

Theorem 4.3.4.4 (Only Complex Matrix satisfying x*Ax=0x^* A x = 0 is the Zero Matrix)

Let A∈Mn×n(𝒞)A \in M_{n\times n}(\mathcal{C}). If for all vectors x∈𝒞nx \in \mathcal{C}^n, we have: x*Ax=0x^* A x = 0 then AA is the zero matrix.

Proof

Let A∈Mn×n(𝒞)A \in M_{n\times n}(\mathcal{C}) be a complex matrix such that for all vectors x∈𝒞nx \in \mathcal{C}^n, we have: x*Ax=0x^* A x = 0 We want to show that AA is the zero matrix.
Take x,y∈𝒞nx, y \in \mathcal{C}^n. Consider the expression: 0=(x+y)*A(x+y)=x*Ax+x*Ay+y*Ax+y*Ay\begin{aligned} 0 &= (x + y)^* A (x + y) \\ &= x^* A x + x^* A y + y^* A x + y^* A y \end{aligned} Since x*Ax=0x^* A x = 0 and y*Ay=0y^* A y = 0 by assumption, we have: 0=x*Ay+y*Ax0 = x^* A y + y^* A x We have - 0=(x+iy)*A(x+iy)0=0x*Ax+ix*Ay−iy*Ax+0y*Ay0=0+ix*Ay−iy*Ax+00=ix*Ay−iy*Ax0=x*Ay−y*Ax\begin{aligned} 0 &= (x + iy)^* A (x + iy) \\ 0 &= 0 x^* A x + i x^* A y - i y^* A x + 0 y^* A y \\ 0 &= 0 + i x^* A y - i y^* A x + 0 \\ 0 &= i x^* A y - i y^* A x \\ 0 &= x^* A y - y^* A x \end{aligned} Combining the two results, we have: x*Ay=0∀x,y∈𝒞n⟹A=0x^* A y = 0 \quad \forall x, y \in \mathcal{C}^n \implies A = 0 ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.5 (Orthogonal Basis wrt Hermitian or Symmetric bilinear Form)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF (either ℝ\mathbb{R} or 𝒞\mathcal{C}), and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric bilinear form (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian form (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}) on VV. Then, there exists an orthogonal basis for VV with respect to the form BB.

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF (either ℝ\mathbb{R} or 𝒞\mathcal{C}), and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric bilinear form (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian form (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}) on VV. We will prove the existence of an orthogonal basis for VV with respect to the form BB using induction on the dimension of VV.
Base Case: If dim⁡(V)=1\dim(V) = 1, then any non-zero vector v∈Vv \in V forms a basis for VV. Since there are no other vectors to compare with, the basis {v}\{v\} is trivially orthogonal with respect to BB.
Inductive Step: Assume that for some k≥1k \geq 1, any vector space of dimension kk has an orthogonal basis with respect to the form BB. We need to show that any vector space of dimension k+1k + 1 also has an orthogonal basis.
Let VV be a vector space of dimension k+1k + 1. Choose a non-zero vector v1∈Vv_1 \in V. If B(v1,v1)=0B(v_1, v_1) = 0, then we can choose another vector until we find one with B(v1,v1)≠0B(v_1, v_1) \neq 0. Now, consider the subspace W={v∈V:B(v,v1)=0}W = \{v \in V : B(v, v_1) = 0\}. The dimension of WW is at least kk since v1v_1 is not in WW. By the inductive hypothesis, there exists an orthogonal basis {v2,v3,…,vk+1}\{v_2, v_3, \ldots, v_{k+1}\} for WW with respect to the form BB.
Now, we claim that the set {v1,v2,v3,…,vk+1}\{v_1, v_2, v_3, \ldots, v_{k+1}\} forms an orthogonal basis for VV with respect to the form BB. We need to verify that B(v1,vi)=0B(v_1, v_i) = 0 for all i=2,3,…,k+1i = 2, 3, \ldots, k + 1. By the definition of WW, we have: B(vi,v1)=0∀i=2,3,…,k+1B(v_i, v_1) = 0 \quad \forall i = 2, 3, \ldots, k + 1 Thus, the set {v1,v2,v3,…,vk+1}\{v_1, v_2, v_3, \ldots, v_{k+1}\} is orthogonal with respect to the form BB. Since it contains k+1k + 1 vectors and spans VV, it forms a basis for VV.
By induction, we conclude that any finite-dimensional vector space VV over a field FF (either ℝ\mathbb{R} or 𝒞\mathcal{C}) has an orthogonal basis with respect to a symmetric bilinear form (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian form (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}) on VV. ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.6 (All Hermitian Matrices are Diagonalizable)

Let A∈Mn(𝒞)A \in M_n(\mathcal{C}) be a Hermitian matrix, i.e., A=A*A = A^*. Then, there exists a unitary matrix P∈GLn(𝒞)P \in GL_n(\mathcal{C}) such that: P*AP=DP^* A P = D where DD is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are only 1, -1, or 0.

Proof

Let A∈Mn(𝒞)A \in M_n(\mathcal{C}) be a Hermitian matrix, i.e., A=A*A = A^*. We want to show that there exists a unitary matrix P∈GLn(𝒞)P \in GL_n(\mathcal{C}) such that: P*AP=DP^* A P = D where DD is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are only 1, -1, or 0.
Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be the standard basis for 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^n. We can represent AA as - A=(⟨ei,ej⟩)i,jA = (\langle e_i, e_j \rangle)_{i,j} where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle is the form associated with AA. By the previous theorem, there exists an orthonormal basis 𝔹1={u1,u2,…,un}\mathbb{B}_1 = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n\} for 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^n with respect to the form ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. Let PP be the matrix whose columns are the vectors of the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1. Since 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is an orthonormal basis, PP is a unitary matrix.
Now, we compute P*APP^* A P P*AP=P*(⟨ei,ej⟩)i,jP=(⟨Pei,Pej⟩)i,j=(⟨ui,uj⟩)i,j\begin{aligned} P^* A P &= P^* (\langle e_i, e_j \rangle)_{i,j} P \\ &= (\langle P e_i, P e_j \rangle)_{i,j} \\ &= (\langle u_i, u_j \rangle)_{i,j} \end{aligned} Since 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is an orthonormal basis, we have ⟨ui,uj⟩=δij\langle u_i, u_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}, where δij\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta. Therefore, the matrix (⟨ui,uj⟩)i,j(\langle u_i, u_j \rangle)_{i,j} is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries equal to 1. Thus, we have: P*AP=DP^* A P = D where DD is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are only 1, -1, or 0. This completes the proof. ◻

Proof

This follows directly from the previous theorem. Given a Hermitian matrix A∈Mn(𝒞)A \in M_n(\mathcal{C}), we know that there exists a unitary matrix P∈GLn(𝒞)P \in GL_n(\mathcal{C}) such that: P*AP=DP^* A P = D where DD is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are only 1, -1, or 0. The columns of the unitary matrix PP form a basis 𝔹\mathbb{B} of 𝒞n\mathcal{C}^n. The matrix representation of the Hermitian form associated with AA with respect to the basis 𝔹\mathbb{B} is given by: [H]𝔹=P*AP=D[H]_{\mathbb{B}} = P^* A P = D Thus, the matrix representation of the Hermitian form associated with AA with respect to the basis 𝔹\mathbb{B} is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries only 1, -1, or 0. ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.7 (det⁡Ak>0\det A_k > 0 for Positive Definite Matrix or Hermition Matrix)

Let A∈Mn×n(F)A \in M_{n \times n}(F) be a symmetric positive definite matrix (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian positive definite matrix (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}). Then, all leading principal minors of AA are positive. That is, for each k=1,2,…,nk = 1, 2, \ldots, n, the determinant of the leading principal submatrix AkA_k is positive: det⁡(Ak)>0\det(A_k) > 0 Where AkA_k is the k×kk \times k submatrix of AA formed by the first kk rows and first kk columns of AA, i.e., Ak=(aij)1≤i,j≤kA_k = (a_{ij})_{1 \leq i,j \leq k} The converse is also true - if all leading principal minors of a symmetric matrix (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian matrix (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}) are positive, then the matrix is positive definite.

Proof

Let A∈Mn×n(F)A \in M_{n \times n}(F) be a symmetric positive definite matrix (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian positive definite matrix (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}). We want to show that all leading principal minors of AA are positive. That is, for each k=1,2,…,nk = 1, 2, \ldots, n, the determinant of the leading principal submatrix AkA_k is positive: det⁡(Ak)>0\det(A_k) > 0 Where AkA_k is the k×kk \times k submatrix of AA formed by the first kk rows and first kk columns of AA.
We show this by induction on kk.
Base Case: For k=1k = 1, the leading principal submatrix A1A_1 is simply the 1×11 \times 1 matrix containing the first entry of AA, i.e., A1=[a11]A_1 = [a_{11}]. Since AA is positive definite, we have: det⁡(A1)=a11>0\det(A_1) = a_{11} > 0 Inductive Step: Assume that for some k≥1k \geq 1, we have det⁡(Ak)>0\det(A_k) > 0. We need to show that det⁡(Ak+1)>0\det(A_{k+1}) > 0.
Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be a basis wrt which AA represents a symmetric bilinear form (if F=ℝF = \mathbb{R}) or a Hermitian form (if F=𝒞F = \mathcal{C}). Let 𝔹1={u1,u2,…,uk+1}\mathbb{B}_1 = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_{k+1}\} be the orthonormal basis for the subspace spanned by the first k+1k+1 basis vectors of 𝔹\mathbb{B}. The matrix representation of the form with respect to the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is given by: [B]𝔹1=P*Ak+1P[B]_{\mathbb{B}_1} = P^* A_{k+1} P where PP is the change of basis matrix from 𝔹\mathbb{B} to 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1. Since 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is an orthonormal basis, the matrix [B]𝔹1[B]_{\mathbb{B}_1} is a diagonal matrix with positive entries on the diagonal. Therefore, we have: det⁡([B]𝔹1)=det⁡(P*Ak+1P)=det⁡(P*)det⁡(Ak+1)det⁡(P)=|det⁡(P)|2det⁡(Ak+1)\begin{aligned} \det([B]_{\mathbb{B}_1}) &= \det(P^* A_{k+1} P) \\ &= \det(P^*) \det(A_{k+1}) \det(P) \\ &= |\det(P)|^2 \det(A_{k+1}) \end{aligned} Since det⁡([B]𝔹1)>0\det([B]_{\mathbb{B}_1}) > 0 and |det⁡(P)|2>0|\det(P)|^2 > 0, it follows that det⁡(Ak+1)>0\det(A_{k+1}) > 0.
By induction, we conclude that all leading principal minors of AA are positive. ◻

Definition 4.3.4.12 (Adjoint Linear Operator)

Let VV be a Hermitian space. Let 𝔹={e1,e2,…,en}\mathbb{B} = \{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n\} be an orthonormal basis for VV. Let T:V→VT: V \to V be a linear operator on VV. The adjoint linear operator of TT, denoted by T*:V→VT^*: V \to V, is the operator assosciated with the conjugate transpose of the matrix representation of TT with respect to the basis 𝔹\mathbb{B}. That is, if [T]𝔹[T]_{\mathbb{B}} is the matrix representation of TT with respect to the basis 𝔹\mathbb{B}, then the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹\mathbb{B} is given by: [T*]𝔹=[T]𝔹*[T^*]_{\mathbb{B}} = [T]_{\mathbb{B}}^*

Definition 4.3.4.13 (Normal Matrix)

A matrix A∈Mn×n(𝒞)A \in M_{n\times n}(\mathcal{C}) is called normal if it commutes with its conjugate transpose. That is, AA is normal if: AA*=A*AA A^* = A^* A

Example 4.3.4.1

Some special cases of normal matrices are:

  • Hermitian Matrices: A=A*A = A^*

  • Unitary Matrices: A*A=AA*=InA^* A = AA^* = I_n

  • Skew-Hermitian Matrices: A=−A*A = -A^*

Theorem 4.3.4.8 (T*T^* is independent of the choice of Orthonormal Basis)

Let VV be a Hermitian space. Let 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 and 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_2 be two orthonormal bases for VV. Let T:V→VT: V \to V be a linear operator on VV. Then, the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V is independent of the choice of orthonormal basis. That is, the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is equal to the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_2.

Proof

Let VV be a Hermitian space. Let 𝔹1={u1,u2,…,un}\mathbb{B}_1 = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n\} and 𝔹2={v1,v2,…,vn}\mathbb{B}_2 = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} be two orthonormal bases for VV. Let T:V→VT: V \to V be a linear operator on VV. We want to show that the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V is independent of the choice of orthonormal basis. That is, we want to show that the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is equal to the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_2.
Let PP be the change of basis matrix from the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 to the basis 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_2. Then, we have: [T]𝔹2=P−1[T]𝔹1P[T]_{\mathbb{B}_2} = P^{-1} [T]_{\mathbb{B}_1} P Taking the conjugate transpose of both sides, we get: [T*]𝔹2=([T]𝔹2)*=(P−1[T]𝔹1P)*=P*[T]𝔹1*(P−1)*=P*[T*]𝔹1(P−1)*\begin{aligned} [T^*]_{\mathbb{B}_2} &= ([T]_{\mathbb{B}_2})^* \\ &= (P^{-1} [T]_{\mathbb{B}_1} P)^* \\ &= P^* [T]_{\mathbb{B}_1}^* (P^{-1})^* \\ &= P^* [T^*]_{\mathbb{B}_1} (P^{-1})^* \end{aligned} Thus, the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_2 is equal to the matrix representation of T*T^* with respect to the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 conjugated by the change of basis matrix PP. Since both bases are orthonormal, the change of basis matrix PP is unitary, and thus the conjugation does not change the operator itself. Therefore, we conclude that the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V is independent of the choice of orthonormal basis. ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.9 (Properties of Adjoint Linear Operator)

Let VV be a Hermitian space. Let T,S:V→VT, S: V \to V be linear operators on VV. Then, the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V satisfies the following properties:

  1. (T+S)*=T*+S*(T + S)^* = T^* + S^*

  2. (cT)*=c¯T*(cT)^* = \overline{c} T^* for all c∈𝒞c \in \mathcal{C}

  3. (TS)*=S*T*(TS)^* = S^* T^*

  4. (T*)*=T(T^*)^* = T

Proof

Let VV be a Hermitian space. Let T,S:V→VT, S: V \to V be linear operators on VV. We want to show that the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V satisfies the following properties:

  1. Additivity: We need to show that (T+S)*=T*+S*(T + S)^* = T^* + S^*. Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be an orthonormal basis for VV. Then, we have: [(T+S)*]𝔹=([T+S]𝔹)*=([T]𝔹+[S]𝔹)*=[T]𝔹*+[S]𝔹*=[T*]𝔹+[S*]𝔹\begin{aligned} [(T + S)^*]_{\mathbb{B}} &= ([T + S]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= ([T]_{\mathbb{B}} + [S]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= [T]_{\mathbb{B}}^* + [S]_{\mathbb{B}}^* \\ &= [T^*]_{\mathbb{B}} + [S^*]_{\mathbb{B}} \end{aligned} Thus, (T+S)*=T*+S*(T + S)^* = T^* + S^*.

  2. Scalar Multiplication: We need to show that (cT)*=c¯T*(cT)^* = \overline{c} T^* for all c∈𝒞c \in \mathcal{C}. Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be an orthonormal basis for VV. Then, we have: [(cT)*]𝔹=([cT]𝔹)*=(c[T]𝔹)*=c¯[T]𝔹*=c¯[T*]𝔹\begin{aligned} [(cT)^*]_{\mathbb{B}} &= ([cT]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= (c[T]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= \overline{c} [T]_{\mathbb{B}}^* \\ &= \overline{c} [T^*]_{\mathbb{B}} \end{aligned} Thus, (cT)*=c¯T*(cT)^* = \overline{c} T^*.

  3. Composition: We need to show that (TS)*=S*T*(TS)^* = S^* T^*. Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be an orthonormal basis for VV. Then, we have: [(TS)*]𝔹=([TS]𝔹)*=([T]𝔹[S]𝔹)*=[S]𝔹*[T]𝔹*=[S*]𝔹[T*]𝔹\begin{aligned} [(TS)^*]_{\mathbb{B}} &= ([TS]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= ([T]_{\mathbb{B}} [S]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= [S]_{\mathbb{B}}^* [T]_{\mathbb{B}}^* \\ &= [S^*]_{\mathbb{B}} [T^*]_{\mathbb{B}} \end{aligned} Thus, (TS)*=S*T*(TS)^* = S^* T^*.

  4. Involution: We need to show that (T*)*=T(T^*)^* = T. Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be an orthonormal basis for VV. Then, we have: [((T*)*)]𝔹=([T*]𝔹)*=([T]𝔹*)*=[T]𝔹\begin{aligned} [((T^*)^*)]_{\mathbb{B}} &= ([T^*]_{\mathbb{B}})^* \\ &= ([T]_{\mathbb{B}}^*)^* \\ &= [T]_{\mathbb{B}} \end{aligned} Thus, (T*)*=T(T^*)^* = T.

 ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.10 (Properties of Adjoint Operators wrt forms on Hermitian Spaces)

Let VV be a Hermitian space with the Hermitian form H:V×V→𝒞H: V \times V \to \mathcal{C}. Let T:V→VT: V \to V be a linear operator on VV. Then, the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V satisfies the following properties with respect to the Hermitian form HH:

  1. H(Tv,w)=H(v,T*w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, w) = H(v, T^* w) \quad \forall v, w \in V

  2. H(Tv,Tw)=H(T*v,T*w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, Tw) = H(T^*v, T^*w) \quad \forall v, w \in V

  3. TT is unitary if and only if H(Tv,Tw)=H(v,w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, Tw) = H(v, w) \quad \forall v, w \in V

  4. TT is Hermitian if and only if H(Tv,w)=H(v,Tw)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, w) = H(v, Tw) \quad \forall v, w \in V

Proof

Let 𝔹\mathbb{B} be an orthonormal basis for VV. We will prove each property one by one. Let the matrix representation of TT with respect to the basis 𝔹\mathbb{B} be denoted by AA, i.e., [T]𝔹=A[T]_{\mathbb{B}} = A.

  1. We need to show that H(Tv,w)=H(v,T*w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, w) = H(v, T^* w) \quad \forall v, w \in V. Let v,w∈Vv, w \in V. Then, we have: H(Tv,w)=(Av)*w=v*A*w=H(v,T*w)\begin{aligned} H(Tv, w) &= (Av)^* w \\ &= v^* A^* w \\ &= H(v, T^* w) \end{aligned}

  2. We need to show that H(Tv,Tw)=H(T*v,T*w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, Tw) = H(T^*v, T^*w) \quad \forall v, w \in V. Let v,w∈Vv, w \in V. Then, we have: H(Tv,Tw)=(Av)*(Aw)=v*A*Aw=H(T*v,T*w)\begin{aligned} H(Tv, Tw) &= (Av)^* (Aw) \\ &= v^* A^* A w \\ &= H(T^*v, T^*w) \end{aligned}

  3. We need to show that TT is unitary if and only if H(Tv,Tw)=H(v,w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, Tw) = H(v, w) \quad \forall v, w \in V.

    • (⇒\Rightarrow) Assume that TT is unitary. Then, we have: A*A=InA^* A = I_n Thus, for any v,w∈Vv, w \in V, we have: H(Tv,Tw)=(Av)*(Aw)=v*A*Aw=v*Inw=H(v,w)\begin{aligned} H(Tv, Tw) &= (Av)^* (Aw) \\ &= v^* A^* A w \\ &= v^* I_n w \\ &= H(v, w) \end{aligned}

    • (⇐\Leftarrow) Assume that H(Tv,Tw)=H(v,w)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, Tw) = H(v, w) \quad \forall v, w \in V. Then, for any v,w∈Vv, w \in V, we have: v*A*Aw=v*wv^* A^* A w = v^* w This implies that: A*A=InA^* A = I_n Thus, TT is unitary.

  4. We need to show that TT is Hermitian if and only if H(Tv,w)=H(v,Tw)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, w) = H(v, Tw) \quad \forall v, w \in V.

    • (⇒\Rightarrow) Assume that TT is Hermitian. Then, we have: A=A*A = A^* Thus, for any v,w∈Vv, w \in V, we have: H(Tv,w)=(Av)*w=v*A*w=v*Aw=H(v,Tw)\begin{aligned} H(Tv, w) &= (Av)^* w \\ &= v^* A^* w \\ &= v^* A w \\ &= H(v, Tw) \end{aligned}

    • (⇐\Leftarrow) Assume that H(Tv,w)=H(v,Tw)∀v,w∈VH(Tv, w) = H(v, Tw) \quad \forall v, w \in V. Then, for any v,w∈Vv, w \in V, we have: v*A*w=v*Awv^* A^* w = v^* A w This implies that: A*=AA^* = A Thus, TT is Hermitian.

Hence proved. ◻

Theorem 4.3.4.11 (Invariant Subspaces under Adjoint Operator)

Let VV be a Hermitian space. Let WW be a subspace of VV that is invariant under a linear operator T:V→VT: V \to V. Then, the orthogonal complement of WW, denoted by W⟂W^\perp, is invariant under the adjoint linear operator T*:V→VT^*: V \to V. That is, T*(W⟂)⊆W⟂T^*(W^\perp) \subseteq W^\perp

Proof

Let u∈W⟂u \in W^\perp. We need to show that T*(u)∈W⟂T^*(u) \in W^\perp. By the definition of orthogonal complement, we have: H(u,w)=0∀w∈WH(u, w) = 0 \quad \forall w \in W Since WW is invariant under TT, we have T(w)∈WT(w) \in W for all w∈Ww \in W. Therefore, we have: H(T*(u),w)=H(u,T(w))=0∀w∈W\begin{aligned} H(T^*(u), w) &= H(u, T(w)) \\ &= 0 \quad \forall w \in W \end{aligned} Hence, T*(u)∈W⟂T^*(u) \in W^\perp. Thus, W⟂W^\perp is invariant under T*T^*.
The converse is also true. Let W⟂W^\perp be invariant under T*T^*. We need to show that WW is invariant under TT. Let w∈Ww \in W. We need to show that T(w)∈WT(w) \in W. By the definition of orthogonal complement, we have: H(u,w)=0∀u∈W⟂H(u, w) = 0 \quad \forall u \in W^\perp Since W⟂W^\perp is invariant under T*T^*, we have T*(u)∈W⟂T^*(u) \in W^\perp for all u∈W⟂u \in W^\perp. Therefore, we have: H(u,T(w))=H(T*(u),w)=0∀u∈W⟂\begin{aligned} H(u, T(w)) &= H(T^*(u), w) \\ &= 0 \quad \forall u \in W^\perp \end{aligned} Hence, T(w)∈WT(w) \in W. Thus, WW is invariant under TT. ◻

4.3.5 Projections

Theorem 4.3.5.1

Let VV be an inner product space with the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. Let WW be a subspace of VV with an orthonormal basis {u1,u2,…,uk}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k\}. Then, for any vector v∈Vv \in V, the projection of vv onto WW is given by: projW(v)=∑i=1k⟨v,ui⟩ui\text{proj}_W(v) = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle v, u_i \rangle u_i

Proof

Let VV be an inner product space with the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. Let WW be a subspace of VV with an orthonormal basis {u1,u2,…,uk}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k\}. We want to show that for any vector v∈Vv \in V, the projection of vv onto WW is given by: projW(v)=∑i=1k⟨v,ui⟩ui\text{proj}_W(v) = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle v, u_i \rangle u_i By the definition of projection, we need to find a vector w∈Ww \in W such that the vector v−wv - w is orthogonal to every vector in WW. Since {u1,u2,…,uk}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k\} is an orthonormal basis for WW, we can express ww as: w=∑i=1kciuiw = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i u_i for some scalars ci∈ℝc_i \in \mathbb{R}. We want to determine the coefficients cic_i such that v−wv - w is orthogonal to each basis vector uju_j for j=1,2,…,kj = 1, 2, \ldots, k. This means we need: ⟨v−w,uj⟩=0∀j=1,2,…,k\langle v - w, u_j \rangle = 0 \quad \forall j = 1, 2, \ldots, k Substituting the expression for ww, we have: ⟨v−∑i=1kciui,uj⟩=0⟨v,uj⟩−∑i=1kci⟨ui,uj⟩=0\begin{aligned} \langle v - \sum_{i=1}^k c_i u_i, u_j \rangle &= 0 \\ \langle v, u_j \rangle - \sum_{i=1}^k c_i \langle u_i, u_j \rangle &= 0 \end{aligned} Since the basis {u1,u2,…,uk}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k\} is orthonormal, we have ⟨ui,uj⟩=δij\langle u_i, u_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}, where δij\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta. Therefore, the above equation simplifies to: ⟨v,uj⟩−cj=0\langle v, u_j \rangle - c_j = 0 for each j=1,2,…,kj = 1, 2, \ldots, k. This gives us: cj=⟨v,uj⟩c_j = \langle v, u_j \rangle for each j=1,2,…,kj = 1, 2, \ldots, k. Substituting these coefficients back into the expression for ww, we get: w=∑i=1k⟨v,ui⟩uiw = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle v, u_i \rangle u_i Thus, the projection of vv onto WW is given by: projW(v)=∑i=1k⟨v,ui⟩ui\text{proj}_W(v) = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle v, u_i \rangle u_i ◻

Definition 4.3.5.1 (Projection of a Vector)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Given a vector v∈Vv \in V and a subspace WW of VV, the projection of vv onto WW, denoted by projW(v)\text{proj}_W(v), is defined as the unique vector w∈Ww \in W such that the vector v−wv - w is orthogonal to every vector in WW. Formally, projW(v)=w∈Wsuch thatB(v−w,u)=0∀u∈W\text{proj}_W(v) = w \in W \quad \text{such that} \quad B(v - w, u) = 0 \quad \forall u \in W

Let 𝔹={e1,e2,…en}\mathbb{B} = \{e_1, e_2, \ldots e_n\} be a basis for RnR^n. Let v∈Rnv \in R^n, and ℙ\mathbb{P} be the plane spanned by {v,ei}\{v, e_i\} for some ii. The projection of vv onto the plane ℙ\mathbb{P} is given by: projℙ(v)=B(v,ei)B(ei,ei)ei\text{proj}_{\mathbb{P}}(v) = \frac{B(v, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i Projections can be thought of as idempotent linear operators on inner product spaces. We have - P:V→V∣P2=PP: V \to V \mid P^2 = P

Theorem 4.3.5.2 (Projection Theorem)

Let VV be an inner product space with the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. Let P:V→VP: V \to V be the projection operator. Then, PP is idempotent and V=Im(P)⊕Ker(P)V = \text{Im}(P) \oplus \text{Ker}(P), where Im(P)\text{Im}(P) is the image of PP and Ker(P)\text{Ker}(P) is the kernel of PP.

Proof

Let v∈Vv \in V. By the definition of projection, we have: P(v)=projW(v)P(v) = \text{proj}_W(v) Applying the projection operator again, we get: P2(v)=P(P(v))=P(projW(v))=projW(projW(v))=projW(v)=P(v)P^2(v) = P(P(v)) = P(\text{proj}_W(v)) = \text{proj}_W(\text{proj}_W(v)) = \text{proj}_W(v) = P(v) Thus, P2=PP^2 = P, proving that PP is idempotent Next, we show that V=Im(P)⊕Ker(P)V = \text{Im}(P) \oplus \text{Ker}(P). Let v∈Vv \in V. We can write vv as: v=P(v)+(v−P(v))v = P(v) + (v - P(v)) Here, P(v)∈Im(P)P(v) \in \text{Im}(P) and v−P(v)∈Ker(P)v - P(v) \in \text{Ker}(P), since: P(v−P(v))=P(v)−P2(v)=P(v)−P(v)=0P(v - P(v)) = P(v) - P^2(v) = P(v) - P(v) = 0 To show that the sum is direct, suppose x∈Im(P)∩Ker(P)x \in \text{Im}(P) \cap \text{Ker}(P). Then, there exists y∈Vy \in V such that x=P(y)x = P(y) and P(x)=0P(x) = 0. Applying PP to both sides of x=P(y)x = P(y), we get: P(x)=P(P(y))=P2(y)=P(y)=xP(x) = P(P(y)) = P^2(y) = P(y) = x Since P(x)=0P(x) = 0, we have x=0x = 0. Thus, Im(P)∩Ker(P)={0}\text{Im}(P) \cap \text{Ker}(P) = \{0\}, proving that the sum is direct. ◻

Theorem 4.3.5.3 (Projection and its Projection Difference are orthogonal)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Given a vector v∈Vv \in V and a subspace WW of VV with an orthonormal basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1, the difference between the vector vv and its projection onto WW is orthogonal the projection itself- (v−projW(v))⟂projW(v)∀v∈V(v - \text{proj}_W(v)) \perp \text{proj}_W(v) \quad \forall v \in V

Proof

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Given a vector v∈Vv \in V and a subspace WW of VV with an orthonormal basis 𝔹1={u1,u2,…,uk}\mathbb{B}_1 = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k\}, we want to show that the difference between the vector vv and its projection onto WW is orthogonal to the projection itself.
By the definition of projection, we have: projW(v)=∑i=1kB(v,ui)ui\text{proj}_W(v) = \sum_{i=1}^k B(v, u_i) u_i Now, we compute the bilinear form between the difference and the projection: B(v−projW(v),projW(v))=B(v−∑i=1kB(v,ui)ui,∑j=1kB(v,uj)uj)=B(v,∑j=1kB(v,uj)uj)−B(∑i=1kB(v,ui)ui,∑j=1kB(v,uj)uj)\begin{aligned} B(v - \text{proj}_W(v), \text{proj}_W(v)) &= B\left(v - \sum_{i=1}^k B(v, u_i) u_i, \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j) u_j\right) \\ &= B\left(v, \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j) u_j\right) - B\left(\sum_{i=1}^k B(v, u_i) u_i, \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j) u_j\right) \end{aligned} Since the basis 𝔹1\mathbb{B}_1 is orthonormal, we have B(ui,uj)=δijB(u_i, u_j) = \delta_{ij}, where δij\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta. Therefore, the second term simplifies to: B(∑i=1kB(v,ui)ui,∑j=1kB(v,uj)uj)=∑i=1k∑j=1kB(v,ui)B(v,uj)B(ui,uj)=∑i=1kB(v,ui)2\begin{aligned} B\left(\sum_{i=1}^k B(v, u_i) u_i, \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j) u_j\right) &= \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_i) B(v, u_j) B(u_i, u_j) \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^k B(v, u_i)^2 \end{aligned} Similarly, the first term becomes: B(v,∑j=1kB(v,uj)uj)=∑j=1kB(v,uj)B(v,uj)=∑j=1kB(v,uj)2\begin{aligned} B\left(v, \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j) u_j\right) &= \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j) B(v, u_j) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j)^2 \end{aligned} Combining these results, we have: B(v−projW(v),projW(v))=∑j=1kB(v,uj)2−∑i=1kB(v,ui)2=0\begin{aligned} B(v - \text{proj}_W(v), \text{proj}_W(v)) &= \sum_{j=1}^k B(v, u_j)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^k B(v, u_i)^2 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned} Thus, we conclude that: (v−projW(v))⟂projW(v)(v - \text{proj}_W(v)) \perp \text{proj}_W(v) for all v∈Vv \in V. ◻

Definition 4.3.5.2 (Angle between Vectors in Inner Product Space)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. The angle θ\theta between two non-zero vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V is defined using the bilinear form BB as follows: cos⁡(θ)=B(u,v)∥u∥B∥v∥B\cos(\theta) = \frac{B(u, v)}{\|u\|_B \|v\|_B} where ∥u∥B\|u\|_B and ∥v∥B\|v\|_B are the lengths of the vectors uu and vv with respect to the bilinear form BB.

This definition generalizes the concept of angles in Euclidean spaces to more general inner product spaces defined by bilinear forms. It allows us to measure the "closeness" or "similarity" between vectors in a way that is consistent with the geometry induced by the bilinear form.

Definition 4.3.5.3 (Reflection)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Given a non-zero vector u∈Vu \in V, the reflection of a vector v∈Vv \in V across the hyperplane orthogonal to uu is defined as: refu(v)=v−2B(v,u)B(u,u)u\text{ref}_u(v) = v - 2 \frac{B(v, u)}{B(u, u)} u

4.4 Properties of Norms Induced by Bilinear Forms

Theorem 4.4.1 (Pythagorean Theorem for Bilinear Forms)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. If u,v∈Vu, v \in V are orthogonal with respect to BB, i.e., B(u,v)=0B(u, v) = 0, then the following holds: ∥u+v∥B2=∥u∥B2+∥v∥B2\|u + v\|_B^2 = \|u\|_B^2 + \|v\|_B^2

Proof

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Let u,v∈Vu, v \in V be orthogonal with respect to BB, i.e., B(u,v)=0B(u, v) = 0. We want to show that: ∥u+v∥B2=∥u∥B2+∥v∥B2\|u + v\|_B^2 = \|u\|_B^2 + \|v\|_B^2 By the definition of the norm induced by the bilinear form BB, we have: ∥u+v∥B2=B(u+v,u+v)=B(u,u)+B(u,v)+B(v,u)+B(v,v)=B(u,u)+0+0+B(v,v)=∥u∥B2+∥v∥B2\begin{aligned} \|u + v\|_B^2 &= B(u + v, u + v) \\ &= B(u, u) + B(u, v) + B(v, u) + B(v, v) \\ &= B(u, u) + 0 + 0 + B(v, v) \\ &= \|u\|_B^2 + \|v\|_B^2 \end{aligned} Hence proved. ◻

Theorem 4.4.2 (Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality for Bilinear Forms)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. For any vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V, the following inequality holds: |B(u,v)|≤∥u∥B∥v∥B|B(u, v)| \leq \|u\|_B \|v\|_B

Proof

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Let u,v∈Vu, v \in V be any vectors. We want to show that: |B(u,v)|≤∥u∥B∥v∥B|B(u, v)| \leq \|u\|_B \|v\|_B Consider the vector w=v−B(u,v)B(u,u)uw = v - \frac{B(u, v)}{B(u, u)} u. We compute the bilinear form B(w,w)B(w, w): B(w,w)=B(v−B(u,v)B(u,u)u,v−B(u,v)B(u,u)u)=B(v,v)−2B(u,v)B(u,u)B(u,v)+(B(u,v)B(u,u))2B(u,u)=B(v,v)−B(u,v)2B(u,u)\begin{aligned} B(w, w) &= B\left(v - \frac{B(u, v)}{B(u, u)} u, v - \frac{B(u, v)}{B(u, u)} u\right) \\ &= B(v, v) - 2 \frac{B(u, v)}{B(u, u)} B(u, v) + \left(\frac{B(u, v)}{B(u, u)}\right)^2 B(u, u) \\ &= B(v, v) - \frac{B(u, v)^2}{B(u, u)} \end{aligned} Since BB is positive definite, we have B(w,w)≥0B(w, w) \geq 0. Therefore, B(v,v)−B(u,v)2B(u,u)≥0B(v, v) - \frac{B(u, v)^2}{B(u, u)} \geq 0 Rearranging this inequality, we get: B(u,v)2≤B(u,u)B(v,v)B(u, v)^2 \leq B(u, u) B(v, v) Taking the square root of both sides, we obtain: |B(u,v)|≤B(u,u)B(v,v)=∥u∥B∥v∥B|B(u, v)| \leq \sqrt{B(u, u)} \sqrt{B(v, v)} = \|u\|_B \|v\|_B Hence proved. ◻

Theorem 4.4.3 (Triangle Inequality for Bilinear Forms)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. For any vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V, the following inequality holds: ∥u+v∥B≤∥u∥B+∥v∥B\|u + v\|_B \leq \|u\|_B + \|v\|_B

Proof

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let B:V×V→FB: V \times V \to F be a symmetric positive definite bilinear form on VV. Let u,v∈Vu, v \in V be any vectors. We want to show that: ∥u+v∥B≤∥u∥B+∥v∥B\|u + v\|_B \leq \|u\|_B + \|v\|_B By the definition of the norm induced by the bilinear form BB, we have: ∥u+v∥B2=B(u+v,u+v)=B(u,u)+B(u,v)+B(v,u)+B(v,v)=∥u∥B2+2B(u,v)+∥v∥B2\begin{aligned} \|u + v\|_B^2 &= B(u + v, u + v) \\ &= B(u, u) + B(u, v) + B(v, u) + B(v, v) \\ &= \|u\|_B^2 + 2B(u, v) + \|v\|_B^2 \end{aligned} Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for bilinear forms, we have: |B(u,v)|≤∥u∥B∥v∥B|B(u, v)| \leq \|u\|_B \|v\|_B Thus, ∥u+v∥B2≤∥u∥B2+2∥u∥B∥v∥B+∥v∥B2=(∥u∥B+∥v∥B)2\begin{aligned} \|u + v\|_B^2 &\leq \|u\|_B^2 + 2\|u\|_B \|v\|_B + \|v\|_B^2 \\ &= (\|u\|_B + \|v\|_B)^2 \end{aligned} Taking the square root of both sides, we obtain: ∥u+v∥B≤∥u∥B+∥v∥B\|u + v\|_B \leq \|u\|_B + \|v\|_B Hence proved. ◻

5 Spectral Theorems and Dual Spaces

5.1 Definitions and Examples

5.1.1 Definitions

The concepts of dual spaces and bilinear forms are fundamental in linear algebra and have wide applications in various fields of mathematics and physics. In this section, we will introduce the definitions and provide examples to illustrate these concepts.

Definition 5.1.1.1 (Linear Functional)

A linear functional on a vector space VV over a field FF is a linear transformation φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F. This means that for all vectors u,v∈Vu, v \in V and scalars c∈Fc \in F, the following properties hold:

  1. φ(u+v)=φ(u)+φ(v)\varphi(u + v) = \varphi(u) + \varphi(v) (additivity)

  2. φ(cu)=cφ(u)\varphi(cu) = c\varphi(u) (homogeneity)

  3. φ(0)=0\varphi(0) = 0 (zero vector maps to zero)

  4. If {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} is a basis for VV, then any linear functional φ\varphi is completely determined by its values on the basis vectors.

Example 5.1.1.1

Let V=ℝ2V = \mathbb{R}^2 be the vector space of all ordered pairs of real numbers. Define a linear functional φ:V→ℝ\varphi: V \to \mathbb{R} by: φ(x,y)=3x+4y\varphi(x, y) = 3x + 4y We can verify that φ\varphi satisfies the properties of a linear functional:

  1. Additivity: For any (x1,y1),(x2,y2)∈V(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2) \in V, φ((x1,y1)+(x2,y2))=φ(x1+x2,y1+y2)=3(x1+x2)+4(y1+y2)=(3x1+4y1)+(3x2+4y2)=φ(x1,y1)+φ(x2,y2)\begin{aligned} \varphi((x_1, y_1) + (x_2, y_2)) &= \varphi(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2) \\ &= 3(x_1 + x_2) + 4(y_1 + y_2) \\ &= (3x_1 + 4y_1) + (3x_2 + 4y_2) \\ &= \varphi(x_1, y_1) + \varphi(x_2, y_2) \end{aligned}

  2. Homogeneity: For any (x,y)∈V(x, y) \in V and scalar c∈ℝc \in \mathbb{R}, φ(c(x,y))=φ(cx,cy)=3(cx)+4(cy)=c(3x+4y)=cφ(x,y)\begin{aligned} \varphi(c(x, y)) &= \varphi(cx, cy) \\ &= 3(cx) + 4(cy) \\ &= c(3x + 4y) \\ &= c\varphi(x, y) \end{aligned}

  3. Zero vector maps to zero: φ(0,0)=3(0)+4(0)=0\varphi(0, 0) = 3(0) + 4(0) = 0

Thus, φ\varphi is a linear functional on V=ℝ2V = \mathbb{R}^2.

Definition 5.1.1.2 (Dual Space)

The dual space of a vector space VV, denoted V*V^*, is the set of all linear functionals on VV. That is, V*={φ:V→F∣φ is a linear functional}V^* = \{\varphi: V \to F \mid \varphi \text{ is a linear functional}\} The dual space V*V^* itself is a vector space over the field FF with the following operations:

  1. Addition: For φ,ψ∈V*\varphi, \psi \in V^*, define (φ+ψ)(v)=φ(v)+ψ(v)(\varphi + \psi)(v) = \varphi(v) + \psi(v) for all v∈Vv \in V.

  2. Scalar Multiplication: For φ∈V*\varphi \in V^* and c∈Fc \in F, define (cφ)(v)=cφ(v)(c\varphi)(v) = c\varphi(v) for all v∈Vv \in V.

  3. Zero Functional: The zero functional 0∈V*0 \in V^* is defined by 0(v)=00(v) = 0 for all v∈Vv \in V.

Example 5.1.1.2

Let V=ℝ3V = \mathbb{R}^3 be the vector space of all ordered triples of real numbers. The dual space V*V^* consists of all linear functionals φ:V→ℝ\varphi: V \to \mathbb{R}. An example of a linear functional in V*V^* is given by: φ(x,y,z)=2x−y+5z\varphi(x, y, z) = 2x - y + 5z We can verify that φ\varphi satisfies the properties of a linear functional:

  1. Additivity: For any (x1,y1,z1),(x2,y2,z2)∈V(x_1, y_1, z_1), (x_2, y_2, z_2) \in V, φ((x1,y1,z1)+(x2,y2,z2))=φ(x1+x2,y1+y2,z1+z2)=2(x1+x2)−(y1+y2)+5(z1+z2)=(2x1−y1+5z1)+(2x2−y2+5z2)=φ(x1,y1,z1)+φ(x2,y2,z2)\begin{aligned} \varphi((x_1, y_1, z_1) + (x_2, y_2, z_2)) &= \varphi(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2, z_1 + z_2) \\ &= 2(x_1 + x_2) - (y_1 + y_2) + 5(z_1 + z_2) \\ &= (2x_1 - y_1 + 5z_1) + (2x_2 - y_2 + 5z_2) \\ &= \varphi(x_1, y_1, z_1) + \varphi(x_2, y_2, z_2) \end{aligned}

  2. Homogeneity: For any (x,y,z)∈V(x, y, z) \in V and scalar c∈ℝc \in \mathbb{R}, φ(c(x,y,z))=φ(cx,cy,cz)=2(cx)−(cy)+5(cz)=c(2x−y+5z)=cφ(x,y,z)\begin{aligned} \varphi(c(x, y, z)) &= \varphi(cx, cy, cz) \\ &= 2(cx) - (cy) + 5(cz) \\ &= c(2x - y + 5z) \\ &= c\varphi(x, y, z) \end{aligned}

  3. Zero vector maps to zero: φ(0,0,0)=2(0)−(0)+5(0)=0\varphi(0, 0, 0) = 2(0) - (0) + 5(0) = 0

Thus, φ\varphi is a linear functional in the dual space V*=(ℝ3)*V^* = (\mathbb{R}^3)^*.

Definition 5.1.1.3 (Hyperplane)

A subspace of a vector space VV over a field FF is called a hyperplane if its dimension is one less than the dimension of VV. Formally, if dim⁡(V)=n\dim(V) = n, then a hyperplane HH in VV satisfies: dim⁡(H)=n−1\dim(H) = n - 1

Theorem 5.1.1.1 (Kernel of a Linear Functional is a Hyperplane)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F be a non-zero linear functional. Then, the kernel of φ\varphi, denoted by Ker(φ)\text{Ker}(\varphi), is a hyperplane in VV. That is, dim⁡(Ker(φ))=dim⁡(V)−1\dim(\text{Ker}(\varphi)) = \dim(V) - 1

Proof

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F be a non-zero linear functional. We want to show that the kernel of φ\varphi, denoted by Ker(φ)\text{Ker}(\varphi), is a hyperplane in VV. That is, we need to show that: dim⁡(Ker(φ))=dim⁡(V)−1\dim(\text{Ker}(\varphi)) = \dim(V) - 1 Since φ\varphi is a non-zero linear functional, there exists at least one vector v0∈Vv_0 \in V such that φ(v0)≠0\varphi(v_0) \neq 0, i.e., dim⁡Im(φ)=1\dim Im (\varphi) = 1. By the Rank-Nullity Theorem, we have: dim⁡(V)=dim⁡(Ker(φ))+dim⁡(Im(φ))\dim(V) = \dim(\text{Ker}(\varphi)) + \dim(Im(\varphi)) Substituting dim⁡(Im(φ))=1\dim(Im(\varphi)) = 1, we get: dim⁡(V)=dim⁡(Ker(φ))+1\dim(V) = \dim(\text{Ker}(\varphi)) + 1 Rearranging this equation, we obtain: dim⁡(Ker(φ))=dim⁡(V)−1\dim(\text{Ker}(\varphi)) = \dim(V) - 1 Thus, the kernel of φ\varphi is a hyperplane in VV. ◻

Now, we can ask the question, is every hyperplane the kernel of some linear functional? The answer is yes, as stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 5.1.1.2 (Hyperplane as Kernel of a Linear Functional)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let HH be a hyperplane in VV. Then, there exists a non-zero linear functional φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F such that the kernel of φ\varphi is exactly HH. That is, Ker(φ)=H\text{Ker}(\varphi) = H

Proof

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let HH be a hyperplane in VV. We want to show that there exists a non-zero linear functional φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F such that the kernel of φ\varphi is exactly HH. That is, we need to find φ\varphi such that: Ker(φ)=H\text{Ker}(\varphi) = H Since HH is a hyperplane in VV, we have: dim⁡(H)=dim⁡(V)−1\dim(H) = \dim(V) - 1 Let {u1,u2,…,un−1}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_{n-1}\} be a basis for HH, where n=dim⁡(V)n = \dim(V). We can extend this basis to a basis for VV by adding one more vector v0∉Hv_0 \notin H. Thus, we have: {u1,u2,…,un−1,v0}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_{n-1}, v_0\} is a basis for VV. Now, we define the linear functional φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F as follows: φ(ui)=0for i=1,2,…,n−1φ(v0)=1\begin{aligned} \varphi(u_i) &= 0 \quad \text{for } i = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1 \\ \varphi(v_0) &= 1 \end{aligned} We need to verify that φ\varphi is a linear functional and that its kernel is exactly HH.

  1. Linearity: For any v,w∈Vv, w \in V and scalar c∈Fc \in F, we can express vv and ww in terms of the basis: v=a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1+bv0w=c1u1+c2u2+…+cn−1un−1+dv0\begin{aligned} v &= a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1} + b v_0 \\ w &= c_1 u_1 + c_2 u_2 + \ldots + c_{n-1} u_{n-1} + d v_0 \end{aligned} Then, φ(v+w)=φ((a1+c1)u1+(a2+c2)u2+…+(an−1+cn−1)un−1+(b+d)v0)=0+0+…+0+(b+d)=b+d=φ(v)+φ(w)\begin{aligned} \varphi(v + w) &= \varphi((a_1 + c_1) u_1 + (a_2 + c_2) u_2 + \ldots + (a_{n-1} + c_{n-1}) u_{n-1} + (b + d) v_0) \\ &= 0 + 0 + \ldots + 0 + (b + d) \\ &= b + d \\ &= \varphi(v) + \varphi(w) \end{aligned} and φ(cv)=φ(c(a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1+bv0))=0+0+…+0+cb=cφ(v)\begin{aligned} \varphi(cv) &= \varphi(c(a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1} + b v_0)) \\ &= 0 + 0 + \ldots + 0 + cb \\ &= c\varphi(v) \end{aligned} Thus, φ\varphi is linear.

  2. Kernel: We need to show that Ker(φ)=H\text{Ker}(\varphi) = H. By definition, the kernel of φ\varphi is given by: Ker(φ)={v∈V∣φ(v)=0}\text{Ker}(\varphi) = \{v \in V \mid \varphi(v) = 0\} Let v∈Hv \in H. Then, we can express vv as: v=a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1v = a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1} Since φ(ui)=0\varphi(u_i) = 0 for all ii, we have: φ(v)=φ(a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1)=0\varphi(v) = \varphi(a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1}) = 0 Thus, v∈Ker(φ)v \in \text{Ker}(\varphi), which shows that H⊆Ker(φ)H \subseteq \text{Ker}(\varphi). Conversely, let v∈Ker(φ)v \in \text{Ker}(\varphi). Then, we can express vv as: v=a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1+bv0v = a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1} + b v_0 Since φ(v)=0\varphi(v) = 0, we have: φ(v)=φ(a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1+bv0)=b=0\varphi(v) = \varphi(a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1} + b v_0) = b = 0 Thus, vv can be expressed as: v=a1u1+a2u2+…+an−1un−1v = a_1 u_1 + a_2 u_2 + \ldots + a_{n-1} u_{n-1} which shows that v∈Hv \in H. Therefore, Ker(φ)⊆H\text{Ker}(\varphi) \subseteq H.

Combining both inclusions, we have Ker(φ)=H\text{Ker}(\varphi) = H. Thus, we have shown that for any hyperplane HH in VV, there exists a non-zero linear functional φ:V→F\varphi: V \to F such that Ker(φ)=H\text{Ker}(\varphi) = H. ◻

Definition 5.1.1.4 (Dual Basis)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF, and let {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} be a basis for VV. The dual basis {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v^1, v^2, \ldots, v^n\} of the dual space V*V^* is defined by the property that: vi(vj)=δijv^i(v_j) = \delta_{ij} for all 1≤i,j≤n1 \leq i, j \leq n, where δij\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta, which is equal to 1 if i=ji = j and 0 otherwise.

Example 5.1.1.3

Let V=ℝ2V = \mathbb{R}^2 be the vector space of all ordered pairs of real numbers. Consider the basis {v1,v2}\{v_1, v_2\} for VV, where: v1=(1,0)v2=(0,1)\begin{aligned} v_1 &= (1, 0) \\ v_2 &= (0, 1) \end{aligned} The dual basis {v1,v2}\{v^1, v^2\} for the dual space V*V^* is defined by the property that: vi(vj)=δijv^i(v_j) = \delta_{ij} for all 1≤i,j≤21 \leq i, j \leq 2. We can define the dual basis vectors as follows: v1(x,y)=xv2(x,y)=y\begin{aligned} v^1(x, y) &= x \\ v^2(x, y) &= y \end{aligned} We can verify that the dual basis satisfies the required property: v1(v1)=v1(1,0)=1v1(v2)=v1(0,1)=0v2(v1)=v2(1,0)=0v2(v2)=v2(0,1)=1\begin{aligned} v^1(v_1) &= v^1(1, 0) = 1 \\ v^1(v_2) &= v^1(0, 1) = 0 \\ v^2(v_1) &= v^2(1, 0) = 0 \\ v^2(v_2) &= v^2(0, 1) = 1 \end{aligned} Thus, the dual basis {v1,v2}\{v^1, v^2\} for the dual space V*V^* is given by: v1(x,y)=xv2(x,y)=y\begin{aligned} v^1(x, y) &= x \\ v^2(x, y) &= y \end{aligned}

Theorem 5.1.1.3 (𝔹*\mathbb{B}^* is a Basis for V*V^*)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF, and let 𝔹={v1,v2,…,vn}\mathbb{B} = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} be a basis for VV. Then, the dual basis 𝔹*={v1,v2,…,vn}\mathbb{B}^* = \{v^1, v^2, \ldots, v^n\} is a basis for the dual space V*V^*.

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF, and let 𝔹={v1,v2,…,vn}\mathbb{B} = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} be a basis for VV. We want to show that the dual basis 𝔹*={v1,v2,…,vn}\mathbb{B}^* = \{v^1, v^2, \ldots, v^n\} is a basis for the dual space V*V^*. To do this, we need to show that 𝔹*\mathbb{B}^* is linearly independent and spans V*V^*.

  1. Linear Independence - Suppose there exist scalars c1,c2,…,cn∈Fc_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n \in F such that: c1v1+c2v2+…+cnvn=0c_1 v^1 + c_2 v^2 + \ldots + c_n v^n = 0 Applying this linear combination to each basis vector vjv_j in 𝔹\mathbb{B}, we get: (c1v1+c2v2+…+cnvn)(vj)=c1v1(vj)+c2v2(vj)+…+cnvn(vj)=c1δ1j+c2δ2j+…+cnδnj=cj\begin{aligned} (c_1 v^1 + c_2 v^2 + \ldots + c_n v^n)(v_j) &= c_1 v^1(v_j) + c_2 v^2(v_j) + \ldots + c_n v^n(v_j) \\ &= c_1 \delta_{1j} + c_2 \delta_{2j} + \ldots + c_n \delta_{nj} \\ &= c_j \end{aligned} Since the left-hand side is equal to 0 for all jj, we have cj=0c_j = 0 for all j=1,2,…,nj = 1, 2, \ldots, n. Thus, the dual basis 𝔹*\mathbb{B}^* is linearly independent.

  2. Spanning - Let φ∈V*\varphi \in V^* be any linear functional. We want to express φ\varphi as a linear combination of the dual basis vectors. For each basis vector viv_i in 𝔹\mathbb{B}, we can compute: φ(vi)=ai\varphi(v_i) = a_i for some scalars ai∈Fa_i \in F. Now, we can express φ\varphi as: φ=a1v1+a2v2+…+anvn\varphi = a_1 v^1 + a_2 v^2 + \ldots + a_n v^n To verify this, we apply the right-hand side to each basis vector vjv_j: (a1v1+a2v2+…+anvn)(vj)=a1v1(vj)+a2v2(vj)+…+anvn(vj)=a1δ1j+a2δ2j+…+anδnj=aj\begin{aligned} (a_1 v^1 + a_2 v^2 + \ldots + a_n v^n)(v_j) &= a_1 v^1(v_j) + a_2 v^2(v_j) + \ldots + a_n v^n(v_j) \\ &= a_1 \delta_{1j} + a_2 \delta_{2j} + \ldots + a_n \delta_{nj} \\ &= a_j \end{aligned} Since this holds for all j=1,2,…,nj = 1, 2, \ldots, n, we have shown that φ\varphi can be expressed as a linear combination of the dual basis vectors. Thus, the dual basis 𝔹*\mathbb{B}^* spans V*V^*.

Since the dual basis 𝔹*\mathbb{B}^* is both linearly independent and spans V*V^*, we conclude that 𝔹*\mathbb{B}^* is a basis for the dual space V*V^*. ◻

5.1.2 Annihilator of a Subset

We now introduce the concept of the annihilator of a subset of a vector space, which is closely related to the dual space.

Definition 5.1.2.1 (Annihilator)

Let VV be a vector space over a field FF, and let S⊆VS \subseteq V. The annihilator of SS, denoted by S0S^0, is defined as the set of all linear functionals φ∈V*\varphi \in V^* such that φ(s)=0\varphi(s) = 0 for all s∈Ss \in S. Formally, S0={φ∈V*∣φ(s)=0,∀s∈S}S^0 = \{\varphi \in V^* \mid \varphi(s) = 0, \forall s \in S\}

Example 5.1.2.1

Let V=ℝ3V = \mathbb{R}^3 be the vector space of all ordered triples of real numbers, and let S={(x,y,0)∣x,y∈ℝ}S = \{(x, y, 0) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{R}\} be a subspace of VV. The annihilator of SS, denoted by S0S^0, consists of all linear functionals φ∈V*\varphi \in V^* such that φ(x,y,0)=0\varphi(x, y, 0) = 0 for all (x,y,0)∈S(x, y, 0) \in S. An example of a linear functional in S0S^0 is given by: φ(x,y,z)=z\varphi(x, y, z) = z We can verify that φ\varphi satisfies the condition for being in the annihilator: φ(x,y,0)=0\varphi(x, y, 0) = 0 Thus, φ\varphi is in the annihilator S0S^0. In fact, the annihilator S0S^0 is spanned by the linear functional φ(x,y,z)=z\varphi(x, y, z) = z, and any linear functional in S0S^0 can be expressed as a scalar multiple of this functional.

Theorem 5.1.2.1 (Dimension of Annihilator)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF, and let SS be a subspace of VV. Then, the dimension of the annihilator of SS, denoted by S0S^0, is given by: dim⁡(S0)=dim⁡(V)−dim⁡(S)\dim(S^0) = \dim(V) - \dim(S)

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF, and let SS be a subspace of VV. We want to show that the dimension of the annihilator of SS, denoted by S0S^0, is given by: dim⁡(S0)=dim⁡(V)−dim⁡(S)\dim(S^0) = \dim(V) - \dim(S) Let 𝔹S={s1,s2,…,sk}\mathbb{B}_S = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_k\} be a basis for the subspace SS, where k=dim⁡(S)k = \dim(S). We can extend this basis to a basis for VV by adding vectors {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v_{k+1}, v_{k+2}, \ldots, v_n\}, where n=dim⁡(V)n = \dim(V). Thus, we have: 𝔹V={s1,s2,…,sk,vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\mathbb{B}_V = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_k, v_{k+1}, v_{k+2}, \ldots, v_n\} is a basis for VV. Now, we can construct the dual basis 𝔹V*={s1,s2,…,sk,vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\mathbb{B}_V^* = \{s^1, s^2, \ldots, s^k, v^{k+1}, v^{k+2}, \ldots, v^n\} for the dual space V*V^*. The annihilator S0S^0 consists of all linear functionals φ∈V*\varphi \in V^* such that φ(si)=0\varphi(s_i) = 0 for all i=1,2,…,ki = 1, 2, \ldots, k. We claim that the set {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v^{k+1}, v^{k+2}, \ldots, v^n\} forms a basis for the annihilator S0S^0. To see this, we first show that these functionals are in S0S^0. For any si∈Ss_i \in S, we have: vj(si)=0for j=k+1,k+2,…,nv^{j}(s_i) = 0 \quad \text{for }j = k+1, k+2, \ldots, n since sis_i is not in the span of {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v_{k+1}, v_{k+2}, \ldots, v_n\}. Thus, each vjv^{j} is in S0S^0. Next, we show that these functionals are linearly independent. Suppose there exist scalars ck+1,ck+2,…,cn∈Fc_{k+1}, c_{k+2}, \ldots, c_n \in F such that: ck+1vk+1+ck+2vk+2+…+cnvn=0c_{k+1} v^{k+1} + c_{k+2} v^{k+2} + \ldots + c_n v^n = 0 Applying this linear combination to each basis vector vjv_j in 𝔹V\mathbb{B}_V, we get: (ck+1vk+1+ck+2vk+2+…+cnvn)(vj)=ck+1vk+1(vj)+ck+2vk+2(vj)+…+cnvn(vj)=cj\begin{aligned} (c_{k+1} v^{k+1} + c_{k+2} v^{k+2} + \ldots + c_n v^n)(v_j) &= c_{k+1} v^{k+1}(v_j) + c_{k+2} v^{k+2}(v_j) + \ldots + c_n v^n(v_j) \\ &= c_j \end{aligned} Since the left-hand side is equal to 0 for all jj, we have cj=0c_j = 0 for all j=k+1,k+2,…,nj = k+1, k+2, \ldots, n. Thus, the set {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v^{k+1}, v^{k+2}, \ldots, v^n\} is linearly independent. Finally, we show that these functionals span S0S^0. Let φ∈S0\varphi \in S^0 be any linear functional. We can express φ\varphi as a linear combination of the dual basis vectors: φ=a1s1+a2s2+…+aksk+bk+1vk+1+bk+2vk+2+…+bnvn\varphi = a_1 s^1 + a_2 s^2 + \ldots + a_k s^k + b_{k+1} v^{k+1} + b_{k+2} v^{k+2} + \ldots + b_n v^n Since φ(si)=0\varphi(s_i) = 0 for all i=1,2,…,ki = 1, 2, \ldots, k, we have: φ(si)=a1s1(si)+a2s2(si)+…+aksk(si)+bk+1vk+1(si)+bk+2vk+2(si)+…+bnvn(si)=ai\begin{aligned} \varphi(s_i) &= a_1 s^1(s_i) + a_2 s^2(s_i) + \ldots + a_k s^k(s_i) + b_{k+1} v^{k+1}(s_i) + b_{k+2} v^{k+2}(s_i) + \ldots + b_n v^n(s_i) \\ &= a_i \end{aligned} Since this holds for all i=1,2,…,ki = 1, 2, \ldots, k, we have ai=0a_i = 0 for all ii. Thus, we can express φ\varphi as: φ=bk+1vk+1+bk+2vk+2+…+bnvn\varphi = b_{k+1} v^{k+1} + b_{k+2} v^{k+2} + \ldots + b_n v^n which shows that φ\varphi is in the span of {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v^{k+1}, v^{k+2}, \ldots, v^n\}. Therefore, the set {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v^{k+1}, v^{k+2}, \ldots, v^n\} spans S0S^0. Combining these results, we conclude that {vk+1,vk+2,…,vn}\{v^{k+1}, v^{k+2}, \ldots, v^n\} is a basis for the annihilator S0S^0. Therefore, the dimension of the annihilator is given by: dim⁡(S0)=n−k=dim⁡(V)−dim⁡(S)\dim(S^0) = n - k = \dim(V) - \dim(S) Hence proved. ◻

Proof

Every hyperplane in VV is the kernel of some linear functional. From the previous theorem, we know that the annihilator S0S^0 of the subspace SS has dimension dim⁡(S0)=dim⁡(V)−dim⁡(S)=n−k\dim(S^0) = \dim(V) - \dim(S) = n - k. Let {φ1,φ2,…,φn−k}\{\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \ldots, \varphi_{n-k}\} be a basis for the annihilator S0S^0. Each linear functional φi\varphi_i defines a hyperplane in VV given by its kernel: Hi=Ker(φi)={v∈V∣φi(v)=0}H_i = \text{Ker}(\varphi_i) = \{v \in V \mid \varphi_i(v) = 0\} Since φi∈S0\varphi_i \in S^0, we have φi(s)=0\varphi_i(s) = 0 for all s∈Ss \in S. Therefore, SS is contained in each hyperplane HiH_i. Now, we claim that: S=H1∩H2∩…∩Hn−kS = H_1 \cap H_2 \cap \ldots \cap H_{n-k} To see this, let v∈H1∩H2∩…∩Hn−kv \in H_1 \cap H_2 \cap \ldots \cap H_{n-k}. Then, φi(v)=0\varphi_i(v) = 0 for all i=1,2,…,n−ki = 1, 2, \ldots, n-k. Since {φ1,φ2,…,φn−k}\{\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \ldots, \varphi_{n-k}\} is a basis for S0S^0, any linear functional in S0S^0 can be expressed as a linear combination of these basis functionals. Therefore, for any φ∈S0\varphi \in S^0, we have: φ(v)=0\varphi(v) = 0 This implies that v∈Sv \in S, since S0S^0 consists of all linear functionals that vanish on SS. Thus, we have shown that: H1∩H2∩…∩Hn−k⊆SH_1 \cap H_2 \cap \ldots \cap H_{n-k} \subseteq S Combining both inclusions, we conclude that: S=H1∩H2∩…∩Hn−kS = H_1 \cap H_2 \cap \ldots \cap H_{n-k} Hence proved. ◻

Theorem 5.1.2.2 (Double Dual Isomorphism)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF. Then, the natural map Φ:V→V**\Phi: V \to V^{**} defined by: Φ(v)(φ)=φ(v)\Phi(v)(\varphi) = \varphi(v) is an isomorphism.

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field FF. We want to show that the natural map Ev:V→V**E_v: V \to V^{**} defined by: Ev(φ)=φ(v)E_v(\varphi) = \varphi(v) is an isomorphism. In other words, we show that V is isomorphic to its double dual V**V^{**}. To do this, we need to show that EvE_v is both linear and bijective.

  1. Linearity - For any φ,ψ∈V*\varphi, \psi \in V^* and scalar c∈Fc \in F, we have: Ev(φ+ψ)=(φ+ψ)(v)=φ(v)+ψ(v)=Ev(φ)+Ev(ψ)Ev(cφ)=(cφ)(v)=cφ(v)=cEv(φ)\begin{aligned} E_v(\varphi + \psi) &= (\varphi + \psi)(v) = \varphi(v) + \psi(v) = E_v(\varphi) + E_v(\psi) \\ E_v(c\varphi) &= (c\varphi)(v) = c\varphi(v) = cE_v(\varphi) \end{aligned} Thus, EvE_v is linear.

  2. Injectivity - Suppose Ev(φ)=0E_v(\varphi) = 0 for some φ∈V*\varphi \in V^*. This means that φ(v)=0\varphi(v) = 0 for all v∈Vv \in V. Since φ\varphi is a linear functional, this implies that φ\varphi is the zero functional. Therefore, EvE_v is injective.

  3. Surjectivity - Let ψ∈V**\psi \in V^{**} be any linear functional on V*V^*. We need to find a vector v∈Vv \in V such that Ev(φ)=ψ(φ)E_v(\varphi) = \psi(\varphi) for all φ∈V*\varphi \in V^*. Since VV is finite-dimensional, we can choose a basis {v1,v2,…,vn}\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\} for VV and let {φ1,φ2,…,φn}\{\varphi^1, \varphi^2, \ldots, \varphi^n\} be the corresponding dual basis for V*V^*. We can express ψ\psi as: ψ=a1φ1+a2φ2+…+anφn\psi = a_1 \varphi^1 + a_2 \varphi^2 + \ldots + a_n \varphi^n for some scalars a1,a2,…,an∈Fa_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in F. Now, we can define the vector vv in VV as: v=a1v1+a2v2+…+anvnv = a_1 v_1 + a_2 v_2 + \ldots + a_n v_n Then, for any φ∈V*\varphi \in V^*, we have: Ev(φ)=φ(v)=φ(a1v1+a2v2+…+anvn)=a1φ(v1)+a2φ(v2)+…+anφ(vn)=a1φ1(v)+a2φ2(v)+…+anφn(v)=ψ(φ)\begin{aligned} E_v(\varphi) &= \varphi(v) \\ &= \varphi(a_1 v_1 + a_2 v_2 + \ldots + a_n v_n) \\ &= a_1 \varphi(v_1) + a_2 \varphi(v_2) + \ldots + a_n \varphi(v_n) \\ &= a_1 \varphi^1(v) + a_2 \varphi^2(v) + \ldots + a_n \varphi^n(v) \\ &= \psi(\varphi) \end{aligned} Thus, EvE_v is surjective.

Since EvE_v is linear, injective, and surjective, we conclude that EvE_v is an isomorphism. Therefore, VV is isomorphic to its double dual V**V^{**}. ◻

5.2 Spectral Theorem

Theorem 5.2.1 (Spectral Theorem for Normal Operators)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional inner product space over the field of complex numbers 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and let T:V→VT: V \to V be a normal operator, i.e., TT*=T*TTT^* = T^*T, where T*T^* is the adjoint of TT. Then, there exists an orthonormal basis of VV consisting of eigenvectors of TT.

We will provide the proof later, after proving some necessary lemmas and definitions.

Theorem 5.2.2 (Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of Adjoint Normal Operators)

Let VV be a finite-dimensional inner product space over the field of complex numbers 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and let T:V→VT: V \to V be a normal linear operator. If λ\lambda is an eigenvalue of TT with corresponding eigenvector vv, then the complex conjugate λ¯\overline{\lambda} is an eigenvalue of the adjoint operator T*T^* with corresponding eigenvector vv.

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional inner product space over the field of complex numbers 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and let T:V→VT: V \to V be a normal linear operator. Suppose λ\lambda is an eigenvalue of TT with corresponding eigenvector vv. This means that: T(v)=λvT(v) = \lambda v We want to show that the complex conjugate λ¯\overline{\lambda} is an eigenvalue of the adjoint operator T*T^* with corresponding eigenvector vv. Let S=T−λIS = T - \lambda I, where II is the identity operator on VV. Then, we have: S(v)=T(v)−λI(v)=λv−λv=0S(v) = T(v) - \lambda I(v) = \lambda v - \lambda v = 0 Let S*=T*−λ¯IS^* = T^* - \overline{\lambda} I be the adjoint of SS. Since TT is normal, we have: SS*=(T−λI)(T*−λ¯I)=TT*−λT*−λ¯T+|λ|2ISS^* = (T - \lambda I)(T^* - \overline{\lambda} I) = TT^* - \lambda T^* - \overline{\lambda} T + |\lambda|^2 I and S*S=(T*−λ¯I)(T−λI)=T*T−λ¯T−λT*+|λ|2IS^*S = (T^* - \overline{\lambda} I)(T - \lambda I) = T^*T - \overline{\lambda} T - \lambda T^* + |\lambda|^2 I Since TT is normal, we have TT*=T*TTT^* = T^*T. Therefore, SS*=S*SSS^* = S^*S. Therefore, we have that SS is also a normal operator. Now, we can compute: S*S(v)=S*(S(v))=S*(0)=0S^*S(v) = S^*(S(v)) = S^*(0) = 0 This implies that vv is in the kernel of S*SS^*S. Since SS is normal, we have: ∥S(v)∥2=⟨S(v),S(v)⟩=⟨S*(v),S*(v)⟩=0\|S(v)\|^2 = \langle S(v), S(v) \rangle = \langle S^*(v), S^*(v) \rangle = 0 Thus, S*(v)=0S^*(v) = 0. Therefore, we have: T*(v)−λ¯I(v)=0T^*(v) - \overline{\lambda} I(v) = 0which implies that: T*(v)=λ¯vT^*(v) = \overline{\lambda} v Thus, λ¯\overline{\lambda} is an eigenvalue of the adjoint operator T*T^* with corresponding eigenvector vv. ◻

5.2.1 Proof of Spectral Theorem

We will now prove the Spectral Theorem for Normal Operators using induction on the dimension of the vector space VV.

Proof

Let VV be a finite-dimensional inner product space over the field of complex numbers 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and let T:V→VT: V \to V be a normal operator. We will prove the Spectral Theorem by induction on the dimension of VV.

  1. Base Case: If dim⁡(V)=1\dim(V) = 1, then any linear operator on VV is a scalar multiple of the identity operator. Thus, TT has an eigenvalue λ\lambda and any non-zero vector in VV is an eigenvector corresponding to λ\lambda. Therefore, the Spectral Theorem holds for dim⁡(V)=1\dim(V) = 1.

  2. Inductive Step: Assume that the Spectral Theorem holds for all inner product spaces of dimension n−1n-1. We will show that it also holds for inner product spaces of dimension nn. Since TT is a linear operator on a finite-dimensional complex vector space, it has at least one eigenvalue λ\lambda. Let vv be a corresponding eigenvector, i.e., T(v)=λvT(v) = \lambda v. Therefore, we have that λ¯\overline{\lambda} is an eigenvalue of the adjoint operator T*T^* with corresponding eigenvector vv. Consider the subspace W=span{v}W = \text{span}\{v\}. We have T(W)⊆WT(W) \subseteq W and T*(W⟂)⊆W⟂T^*(W^\perp) \subseteq W^\perp. Where W⟂W^\perp is the orthogonal complement of WW, denoted by W⟂W^\perp. Since TT is normal on W⟂W^\perp and dim⁡(W⟂)=n−1\dim(W^\perp) = n-1, by the inductive hypothesis, there exists an orthonormal basis of W⟂W^\perp consisting of eigenvectors of T|W⟂T|_{W^\perp}. Let {u1,u2,…,un−1}\{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_{n-1}\} be this orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of T|W⟂T|_{W^\perp}. Now, we can extend this basis to an orthonormal basis of VV by adding the vector vv. Thus, we have: {v,u1,u2,…,un−1}\{v, u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_{n-1}\} is an orthonormal basis of VV. Since vv is an eigenvector of TT corresponding to the eigenvalue λ\lambda, and each uiu_i is an eigenvector of T|W⟂T|_{W^\perp}, we conclude that the entire basis consists of eigenvectors of TT. Therefore, the Spectral Theorem holds for dim⁡(V)=n\dim(V) = n.

Hence, by the principle of mathematical induction, the Spectral Theorem holds for all finite-dimensional inner product spaces over the field of complex numbers 𝒞\mathcal{C}. ◻

We have now completed the proof of the Spectral Theorem for Normal Operators. This concludes the notes for the course MA2102 - Linear Algebra I.
